To determine whether TRM cell activation requires epithelial invasion or only luminal exposure to the pathogen, we leveraged the S.Tm mutants introduced previously (ΔFg, ΔSPI-2 and ΔSPI-1/2; Fig. 3). We found that the extent of mucosal injury and the magnitude of TRM cell response correlated with S.Tm invasive capacity and epithelial IL-18 secretion (Fig. 5e,f and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Furthermore, in line with the stronger epithelial response described earlier (Extended Data Fig. 8g), S.Tm SL1344 induced a more rapid and severe immunopathology than S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 10h). Together, these data link TRM cell responses to pathogen virulence, invasive capacity and subsequent epithelial cytokine secretion. Although TRM cell responses are classically defined by antigen-specific TCRs, their capacity for innate-like bystander responses is a critical yet poorly understood feature of human mucosal immunity. We sought to understand whether S.Tm-mediated TRM cell activation is driven by secreted epithelial signals rather than direct TCR binding to epithelial MHC. Inhibition of PI3K and p38 MAPK, essential for innate-like IFNγ induction50, significantly quelled the response, whereas TCR-dependent LCK inhibition51 indicated no effect (Fig. 5g). Likewise, surface TCR expression remained stable during S.Tm infection, contrasting the expected downregulation triggered by synthetic TCR engagement via an EpCAM–CD3 bispecific52 (Fig. 5h). Conditioned media from infected epithelium-only barriers were sufficient to activate TRM cells, whereas direct stimulation with bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (LPS and flagellin) failed to trigger degranulation (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10i). We note that this non-cognate response appeared to be a hallmark of tissue residency, as allogeneic and autologous blood-derived T cells remained unresponsive to infection, despite exhibiting substantial CD45RO+ populations (Extended Data Fig. 9d), high viability and IL-2 induction capacity (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these results establish S.Tm-induced TRM cell activation in this system as a TCR-independent bystander response that requires inflammatory signals relayed by the epithelium. The induction of IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion closely coincided with the kinetics of the T cell response (Fig. 5d), implicating this cytokine as a key epithelial orchestrator of T cell activation. This was supported by high expression of IL-18Rα on CD4+ TRM cells, which conferred pronounced responsiveness to exogenous IL-18 and S.Tm infection (Fig. 5j and Extended Data Fig. 10l,m). To assess its role as an epithelial messenger, we generated IL18 knockouts in intestinal organoids using CRISPR–Cas9, resulting in ablation of IL-18 expression at baseline and upon challenge (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 10n). Indeed, IL-18 levels in WT S.Tm-infected mutant barriers were comparable with those of the avirulent ΔSPI-1/2 infection and non-infected control (Fig. 5l). When assessing the TRM cell response, IL-18 deficiency significantly dampened the inflammatory response (Fig. 5l,m), attenuating intracellular IFNγ levels in the cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ responder population (Extended Data Fig. 10o). Critically, the loss of IL-18 protected the barrier from pathological shedding and thinning (Fig. 5n and Extended Data Fig. 10p) despite functional T cell responder potential, linking IL-18-driven T cell activation to immunopathology.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the epithelium orchestrates antibacterial mucosal defence by secreting IL-18 to trigger non-cognate, innate-like responses of the TRM compartment.

According to recent reports, we have reported bioengineered, luminally accessible human intestinal tissues comprising epithelia with periodically repeating crypts that maintain LGR5+ stem cells, in vivo-like cell composition and patterning, and retain transcriptomic signatures across multiple donors. Identical medium and biophysical culture conditions yield region-specific signatures due to stem cell origin. Cell-type maturation and a reduction in total apical volume enable the formation of a region-specific mucus layer with mature glycocalyx. In addition, autologous TRM cells patrol the barrier and engage in bidirectional crosstalk with the epithelium, conferring an immune-responsive state within epithelial cells via IFNγ signalling.

Recent findings suggest that the modularity of the system enabled newly introduced inquiry into S.Tm infection in a human context, contributing to collective efforts to refine physiologically relevant enteric infection models53. Basolateral S.Tm localization within polarized cells presumably facilitates dissemination into the lamina propria, a phenomenon that has been reported in vivo54,55. In addition, the phenotypic divergence observed between SL1344 and 14028 strains could expand to clinical isolates and human-restricted pathogens (for example, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi, Shigella flexneri and Vibrio cholerae), including the study of host factors influencing bacterial gene expression and antibiotic susceptibility. We mapped the gene regulatory networks underlying luminal and intracellular S.Tm at single-cell resolution. The epithelium orchestrated inflammatory, metabolic and structural responses that accompany S.Tm colonization26 and demonstrate an innate-sensing capacity that coordinates multi-lineage immune recruitment in vivo. S.Tm invasion reshaped the host transcriptome through a SteE-dependent STAT3 gene regulatory hub that extends results in macrophages and immortalized lines29,31. The reduced SPI-2 contribution may stem from non-transcriptional effector roles or delayed activation resulting from the SPI-1-inducing pre-culture protocol56. In addition, changes in oxidative stress and iron homeostasis suggest a host–pathogen interplay associated with other intracellular infections57, warranting further study. Overall, these responses were highly influenced by the intracellular burden of the pathogen.

Industry observers note that advancing our previous work40 to an apically accessible immunocompetent system, we demonstrated that epithelial IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion is sufficient to drive TRM cell activation and cytokine release, reflecting clinical gastroenteric salmonellosis48,49. The system allowed us to elucidate the functional effects of this bystander T cell activation, aligning with previous reports of innate-like polyfunctional capabilities of TRM cells58,59,60. TRM cells intensified infection-mediated epithelial shedding, which probably contributes to pathogen clearance61 and is consistent with the rapid onset of diarrhoea during S.Tm infection. Although mouse studies have established the necessity of IL-18 for CD4+ T cell defence upon S.Tm infection62, it has been shown that enteric neurons, rather than the epithelium, serve as the critical source of IL-18 for intestinal protection63. We demonstrated that the human intestinal epithelium can potently activate TRM cells via IL-18 to drive defence responses, at least in an in vitro setting. Of note, S.Tm infection64 and IL-18 (ref. 65) have been linked to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. Our data raise the possibility that this association may be underpinned by the appearance of a cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ T cell population58,62.

Although our platform provides a unique window into human intestinal in vitro modelling, several limitations remain. The engineered tissues lack villous structures, specialized Paneth or M cells, and myeloid immune lineages, crucial mediators of immunity against infection. The lack of fluid exchange might affect biophysical characteristics of a mucus layer accumulated by apical media reduction. Furthermore, S.Tm invasion rates probably exceed physiological levels due to mucus protection. Future studies may circumvent these limitations through bioengineering approaches9, mucus secretagogues, cytokine supplementation or the inclusion of additional commensal and immune lineages.

Beyond host–pathogen interaction, the engineered tissues and analytical framework expand what can be addressed ex vivo. The mature, patterned epithelium opens research directions in region-specific drugs and nutrient absorption, mucus biology and epithelial–TRM cell interactions implicated in inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis. Overall, the platform brings the field closer to capturing complex, organ-level processes in a human setting that is controllable and tractable.

During the work on this project, a large number of microdevice prototype versions were fabricated using a range of microfabrication techniques, including cleanroom soft lithography, 3D printing, two-photon polymerization (2PP) lithography, computer numerical control (CNC) milling and plastic injection molding. The final chip is designed in a slide format (75 × 25 mm) containing three independent chips per slide. Each chip contained a central hydrogel chamber flanked by two side medium reservoirs and one top medium reservoir. The hydrogel precursor was injected through a loading port leading to the central gel chamber. A cylindrical stamp with a microtopography (for example, an array of biomimetic micropillars) on its base was placed onto a stamp-holding edge of the top reservoir before gel injection. After gel polymerization (see details in a separate section), the stamp was removed, leaving an inverse microtopography (for example, an array of microwells) on the hydrogel surface. The top and side reservoirs were then filled with PBS or cell culture medium. The top reservoir was used for cell seeding and subsequently served as the apical medium reservoir after epithelial coverage of the hydrogel and barrier formation. Medium from the side reservoirs passively diffused through the gel, supplying the epithelial tissue with nutrients from the basal side. Early prototypes were fabricated using conventional soft lithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) molding workflows established at the Center of Micronanotechnology (EPFL). The 3D chip design was split into two photomasks that were sequentially aligned to enable the creation of pseudo-3D features and different heights for phase-guiding micro-pillars. Chip layouts were patterned onto chrome-coated fused silica substrates via laser lithography (VPG200, Heidelberg Instruments). Three layers of SU8 GM1075 (Gerlteltec) were sequentially spin coated onto dehydrated silicon wafers to achieve a total mold thickness of 750 μm. The first two 250-μm layers were soft baked, exposed to UV through the first photomask (MA6/BA6, Süss MicroTec) and post-baked. Then, the third SU8 layer was spin coated, soft baked and the second photomask was aligned to the existing pattern using dedicated alignment marks. After a final post-exposure bake and development with propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA; Sigma), the molds were hard baked at 135 °C for 4 h and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was mixed at a 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio, poured onto the molds, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 24 h. PDMS replicas were cut, punched and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. The strength of the soft lithography pipeline is in fabrication of high-resolution microfeatures and with relatively optimal throughput, as 10–20 chips can be produced from a single wafer. However, fabrication of the models taller than 500 μm is challenging and only step-like, pseudo-3D features from a single side of the PDMS layer can be fabricated. To overcome these limitations, we explored several other complementary fabrication strategies. Commercial 3D-printing techniques such as fused deposition modelling and stereolithography were used for the production of larger models (Formlabs Form 4). However, these methods lacked the resolution and surface finish required for high-quality PDMS molding and were suitable only for some early-stage proof-of-concept prototypes. Instead, here we used 2PP lithography using the UpNano NanoOne printer to fabricate detailed 3D features of the chip. In brief, 3D models of the microchip were created in Autodesk Fusion (latest version), exported as STL files and processed using UpNano Think3D software. The models were printed on glass coverslips using UpPhoto resin (UpNano). NanoOne stands out as the most developed printer for mesoscale manufacturing, enabling printing of large structures (10–20 mm in xy and up to 40 mm in height) due to several advanced technologies: a submerged printing mode in a large resin reservoir, high-power 1,000 W, 780-nm laser for fast printing with 5 × 0.25 numerical aperture (NA) objective and adaptive resolution technology that significantly reduces print times (up to 450 mm3 h−1). After printing, the coverslips were washed in isopropanol and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS was cast, degassed, cured at 80 °C and then replicas were cut and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This method allowed us to fabricate high-quality prototypes for validation of the 3D microstructural design elements. However, the main limitation is the upscaling technology for fabrication of the large number of chips. More importantly, process flow is still resulting in the 3D topography features only from one side of the PDMS replica. To overcome the latter problem, commonly some laboratories fabricate multi-layered PDMS chips. In this approach, individual PDMS layers are fabricated separately, aligned and plasma bonded together. This direction was explored early on for fabrication of a few prototypes; however, the alignment process is tedious and unsuitable for large-scale chip manufacturing with the acceptable quality. To address this, inspired by industrial injection molding technology, we developed a cassette mold for PDMS curing. Molds were manufactured by CNC milling of acrylic, aluminum or steel, depending on the desired feature size and quality. Each cassette consisted of two mold parts bearing microtopographies of the bottom and top surfaces of the chip. When assembled, the parts fit precisely, enabling accurate alignment of both sides of the device. PDMS was injected into centre space of the mold, degassed in a vacuum chamber and cured in an 80 °C oven. After curing, the mold was opened and the PDMS sheets were cut and bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This process overcomes many of the limitations of previously described techniques and enables scalable production of hundreds of high-quality chips in a single batch. The main drawback is the need to adapt design features for CNC milling: some of the smallest features must be enlarged and sharp corners rounded. However, we did not consider this as a drawback as concurrently we began exploring industrial plastic molding technologies to eliminate the last remaining problem: the PDMS material itself. Although PDMS is ideal for prototyping, its high absorption of small molecules makes it unsuitable for translational applications and drug testing. Many of the learnings and design optimizations from the PDMS cassette-molding process were directly translated into the design of the final injection-molded plastic chip. Currently, the chip body is fabricated from cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) due to its low shrinkage, chemical resistance and optical transmission. The main body was fabricated as a single piece, followed by bonding of a 170-μm COC film to the bottom surface. A matching lid converting the slide was later designed and produced separately also via a COC injection molding process. After assembly, chips were packaged and sterilized using ethylene oxide gas. Large-scale chip production was outsourced to an external manufacturing facility.

It has been revealed that stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS via replica molding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion (latest version). Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consisted of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 70 to 120 μm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 μm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a 10 × 0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mold with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mold for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

To generate the ECM for the chip bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized following the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) in 87.5:12.5 (v/v) ratio. A PDMS stamp with crypt-mimmicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir. After the gel injection through the gel-loading port, the hydrogel was polymerized on a 37 °C hotplate for 10 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium. Prepared chips with hydrogels can be stored for multiple weeks at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as ‘incubator’) or in the +4 °C fridge before use. Hydrogel stiffness was measured using an MCR 702e MultiDrive oscillatory shear rheometer (Anton Paar) in a parallel plate configuration with a PP25/P3 measuring plate. The Young’s modulus (E) was estimated from the storage modulus (G′), assuming the hydrogel is elastic and nearly incompressible, using the relation E = 2 G(1 + ν) ≈ 3 G′, where Poisson’s ratio (ν) is approximately 0.5. Across multiple batches and replicates, the hydrogels yielded a Young’s modulus of 3,000 ± 500 Pa.

Industry observers note that in brief, intestinal tissue was processed by removal of the underlying muscularis, serosa and fat from the basal side of the intestinal tissue using forceps and scissors. The remaining mucosal tissue was thoroughly washed with DPBS (10010-015, Gibco), supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin (1,500 U ml−1; 15140122, Gibco), gentamicin (500 µg ml−1; 15750060, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and primocin (50 µg ml−1; ant-pm1, Invivogen) before using a glass coverslip to remove excess mucus from the luminal side and blood vessels from the basal side.

It has been revealed that to circumvent the poor viability and phenotypic alterations associated with traditional enzymatic disassociations66,67, we adapted and optimized a scaffold-based egression method68 that we have previously shown maximizes tissue-resident immune cell recovery and maintains phenotypic integrity40. As previously reported40, our characterization via scRNA-seq and flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that the vast majority of the isolated cells are TRM cells. Therefore, we used the term TRM cells to describe the total immune cell fraction isolated from intestinal tissue. By flow cytometry, we characterized them as TRM cells based on the assessment of one or multiple of the following markers CD45RO+, CD69+, CD103+, CD45RA− and CCR7−.

According to recent reports, cleaned tissue was cut into square pieces (approximately 5 × 5 mm3) with a scalpel. Next, each fragment was loaded onto a 9 × 9 × 1.5 mm3 tantalum-coated, carbon-based scaffold (MSPP23281-1-REV-A, Ultramet) and cultured in 24-well plates (CC7682-7524, CytoOne) containing 2 ml of cytokine-free immune medium (Supplementary Table 1). Twenty-four hours later, scaffolds with tissue on were removed, and egressed cells were harvested from the bottom of the wells by thorough pipetting. Cells were then counted and biobanked in CryoStor (C2874, Sigma-Aldrich) before further use.

For isolation of donor-matched crypts for organoid establishment, an adjacent clean tissue piece (approximately 3 cm2) was used. Intestinal villi were removed from the tissue by using a glass coverslip. The tissue was then incubated on ice in DPBS + 10 mM EDTA (15575020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a shaker for 30 min. Next, a coverslip was used to scrape off the crypts of the tissue. Crypts were collected in organoid medium (Supplementary Table 1). Crypts were centrifuged and resuspended in GFR Matrigel (356231, Corning). After polymerization for 15 min at 37 °C, organoid medium was added with 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies). Following organoid formation, organoids were passaged every 7 days (up to a maximum of 25 passages). After three passages, organoid mycoplasma tests (LT07-710, Lonza) were performed. All lines used in this study were verified as negative for mycoplasma. Organoid banking was performed using CELLBANKER 1 (11888, Nippon Zenyaku Kogyo). Passaging was performed as previously described52. In brief, organoid medium was removed and wells were washed with DPBS. Next, 500 µl of Gentle Cell Dissociation reagent (07174, Stemcell Technologies) was added and incubated for 2 min at room temperature before collecting the domes in a Falcon tube. After a further 15 min of incubation at room temperature, the suspension was centrifuged at 350g at 4 °C for 5 min. After removal of liquid, the pellet was harshly resuspended with organoid wash medium (Supplementary Table 1) to break the organoids. Broken organoids were centrifuged at 500g and the supernatant discarded before pellet resuspension in GFR Matrigel.

To generate LGR5, CDH1 and H2BC4 reporter lines, targeting vectors were designed as previously described69. Human intestinal organoids were incubated with 1.25% DMSO (v/v) and 10 µM Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) 24 h before electroporation. Organoids (amounting to approximately 1 million cells per condition) were harvested, dissociated to clumps of 3–5 cells with TrypLE (12604-013, Gibco), washed twice with Optimem (31985070, Gibco) and then resuspended in High Performance Electroporation Solution (45-0805, BTXpress) containing up to 10 µg of targeting vector and 10 µg of Cas9 and guide RNA-expressing vector. Cells were electroporated using the NEPA21 Super Electroporator (Nepagene) with settings as previously described70. Y-27632 was kept for 48 h post-single-cell seeding in growth factor-reduced Matrigel (356231, Corning). Reporter-positive organoids were either picked manually or enriched via FACS.

Industry observers note that to generate IL-18 gene knockouts, cells were transfected with 20 µg Cas9–GFP and guide RNA expression constructs at a 1:8 ratio and incubated overnight in culture medium containing 5% Matrigel. Transfected cells were FACS enriched and allowed to grow for 10–14 days. Up to eight clones were manually picked and genotyped by Sanger sequencing of the targeted locus.

Sources indicate that S.Tm NCTC 12023 (identical to ATCC14028) and SL1344 WT and isogenic mutant strains were used as listed in Supplementary Table 1. If required for detection of Salmonella by GFP expression, plasmid pFPV25.1 was introduced by electroporation and maintained by selection with 50 µg ml−1 carbenicillin (Roth).

Recent findings suggest that mutant strains with deletion in invG or steE were generated by λ-Red recombination as previously described71 using pKD13 as template for amplification with Del13 primer sets (synthesized by IDT) listed in Supplementary Table 1, and pWRG730 for expression for λ-Red recombinase functions72. Proper insertion of the aph resistance cassette in target genes was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck for primers and K1 Red-Del. If required, the aph resistance cassette was removed by FLP recombination mediated by helper plasmid pE-FLP73. Resulting clones were checked for loss of kanamycin resistance and pE-FLP, and FLP-mediated deletion was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck For/Rev primer sets.

Strain MvP3487 was generated by P22 transduction of the ΔssaV::aph allele into MvP1764 according to standard procedures. Resulting mutant strains were checked for the absence of lysogens.

For seeding of the chips—hereafter referred to as ‘engineered intestines’ once intestinal epithelial cells are included—approximately 4-day-old human intestinal organoids from different regions of the gastrointestinal tract (duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon) between passages 5 and 25 were collected in base medium (Supplementary Table 1) and transferred to a 15-ml Falcon tube. Following centrifugation at 300g at 4 °C for 4 min, the base medium was aspirated and the pellet was thoroughly resuspended in base medium. After repeating the centrifugation step, organoids were singularized with TrypLE express solution (12604-013, Gibco) containing 250 U ml−1 DNase I (4536282001, Roche) and 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) for 8 min at 37 °C before harsh resuspension. This step was performed twice before swiftly blocking the dissociation by adding base medium with 10% FBS. Next, cells were passed through a 40-µm strainer (43-50040-51, PluriSelect) before centrifugation at 500g at 4 °C for 4 min. Afterwards, the cells were resuspended in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) containing 10 µm Y-27632. Approximately 1.5 × 105 cells were seeded in a volume of 3 µl onto each micropatterned hydrogel. Approximately 150 µl chip medium with 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestines, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow the cells to attach to the ECM. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl chip medium (+10 µm Y-27632 + 5% FBS) was carefully added to the mid-chamber to avoid cell detachment. Culture medium was exchanged every second day. Approximately 5% of FBS supplementation was removed after the second day (details in Supplementary Table 1).

According to recent reports, on the day of hydrogel seeding, TRM cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells were thawed following our previously described protocol52. T cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells using the EasySep Human T Cell Isolation kit (17951, Stemcell Technologies) and EasySep Magnet (18000, Stemcell Technologies) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Viability and number of immune cells were assessed with Trypan Blue (216040, Invitrogen) on a Countess II (Invitrogen). If the viability of the thawed TRM cells crawl-out was less than 75% (due to remaining tissue debris), Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was applied with MS columns (130-042-201, Miltenyi Biotec) on the OctoMACS separator (130-042-109, Miltenyi Biotec) following the manufacturer’s instructions (typically improved to more than 85% viability). Afterwards, immune cells were placed in the incubator until further processing. Chips were prepared as described above until hydrogel loading. Then, approximately 1 × 105 immune cells were mixed with 6 µl of ECM per chip. Next, 26 µl of ECM was dispensed through the loading port per chip into the mid-reservoir. Immediately after, 6 µl of the ECM-immune suspension was carefully dispensed onto a flipped PDMS stamp, with the micropattern facing upwards, and transferred using forceps onto the previously dispensed ECM in the mid-reservoir of the engineered intestine. Next, immune-hydrogel suspensions were polymerized at 37 °C for 15 min. After polymerization of the ECM, the immune chip slide was topped up with immune chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to ease microstamp removal. After organoid dissociation and epithelial cell seeding as described above, 150 µl immune chip medium containing 500 pg ml−1 IL-15 (570306, BioLegend) and 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestine, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow for cells to attach to the ECM of the engineered intestine. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15 + 10 µm Y-27632) was carefully added to the mid-chamber. Immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15) was exchanged every second day.

Sources indicate that to assess the effects of bacterial components on TRM cells in suspension, LPS (100 ng ml−1; L3024-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and flagellin (50 ng ml−1; tlrl-epstfla-5, InvivoGen) were supplemented in immune medium and cultured for 48 h. Similarly, IL-15 (500 pg ml−1) and IL-18 (10 ng ml−1; 592106, BioLegend) were added in immune medium for TRM cell suspension cultures, either individually or in combination, for 48 h. For the assessment of T cell activation in response to the epithelial secretome, conditioned medium was harvested from the basal reservoirs of epithelium-only chips 48 hpi with S.Tm. This medium was collected, transferred to plates and maintained at −80 °C until the day of the experiment. Upon thawing, condition medium was mixed 1:1 (v/v) with fresh immune medium supplemented with 1,000 pg ml−1 of IL-15, resulting in a final concentration of 500 pg ml−1 of IL-15. TRM cells were subsequently cultured in this mixture for 48 h in suspension. Following these culture periods, cells were subjected to analysis by flow cytometry.

Industry observers note that for baseline phenotyping, immune cells were recovered from intestinal resections, filtered through a 40-µm strainer and processed directly. For assessment of luminal content, cells were recovered from the accessible luminal reservoir of the chips. For chip-harvested samples and suspension-cultured TRM cells intended for intracellular cytokine assessment, samples were treated with a protein transport inhibitor cocktail (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h before harvest. To achieve single-cell suspension of tissues for staining, samples were retrieved via a 3-mm biopsy punch and transferred to warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1; 11088858001, Millipore) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1; T9128, Sigma). Samples were incubated in a shaker (1,000 rpm at 37 °C) for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. Following visible disintegration, cells were centrifuged (500g for 3 min), resuspended in Accutase with DNAse I (40 U ml−1) and incubated for 10 min at room temperature until a single-cell suspension was achieved. All samples were filtered (40 µm) and washed twice in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS) before staining.

Sources indicate that cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) in Brilliant Stain Buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) for 10 min at room temperature in PBS, followed by a fixable viability dye in PBS (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher) for 10 min following centrifugation. Surface antibodies were applied in FACS buffer for 15 min at room temperature. Following centrifugation and surface labelling, samples were processed according to their experimental requirement. Baseline samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 min at room temperature. Intracellular cytokine samples were fixed using IC fixation buffer (30 min in the dark at room temperature; 15284728, Invitrogen), washed in 1X permeabilization buffer (15284728, Invitrogen) and incubated with intracellular antibodies for 30 min at room temperature. Finally, samples were washed once more in 1X permeabilization buffer before centrifugation.

In a recent development, cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) and brilliant stain buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) in FACS buffer for 15 min at 4 °C. Without washing, a 2X concentrated antibody master mix of chemokine receptors (CX3CR1, CXCR5, CCR7 and CD103) was added directly and incubated for 20 min at 37 °C in the incubator. Following centrifugation, the remaining surface antibodies and streptavidin were applied in FACS buffer for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by a single wash with PBS and centrifugation. Viability dye was then added in PBS for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by centrifugation. To fix and permeabilize the cells for intracellular cytokine and transcription factor staining, the FoxP3 kit (00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions (30 min at 4 °C). Following centrifugation, intracellular antibodies were prepared in 1X permeabilization buffer and incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. Finally, samples were washed twice in 1X permeabilization buffer before the final centrifugation and acquisition.

Sources indicate that final cell suspensions were resuspended in 150 µl FACS buffer and acquired on a BD Fortessa or a Cytek Aurora (five-laser configuration). Data were analysed using FlowJo (v10; BD Biosciences) and OMIQ (v1.22; Dotmatics). All surface and intracellular staining antibodies can be found in Supplementary Table 1.

Industry observers note that from the raw data acquired by flow cytometry, using FlowJo software (v10.10; BD Biosciences), live CD45+ cells were identified using manual gating. For flow-cytometry data, the compensation matrix was corrected in FlowJo (BD Biosciences) by pre-gating on live immune cells, and the total fraction of live singlet immune cells was exported. Data were then transformed with an inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) function (cofactors ranging between 400 and 10,000), then imported into the OMIQ environment (v1.22; Dotmatics) for subsequent analysis.

Recent findings suggest that the high-dimensional analysis was carried out based on the workflow previously described74. In brief, UMAPs75 were generated, and FlowSOM clustering76 was overlaid on the dimensionality reduction maps. Frequency plots were generated downstream of manual gating outputs using Prism (v10.6.1).

To assess the barrier integrity of the engineered epithelia in homeostatic conditions, the apical and basal media were aspirated thoroughly. Next, 120 µl of a 100 µg ml−1 solution of Cascade Blue hydrazide, trilithium salt (C3239, Invitrogen) in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) was added to the apical reservoir. Of chip medium without Cascade Blue, 170 µl was added to the side reservoirs. The assay was carried out for 180 min in the incubator. Subsequently, the fluorescence of the basal medium was quantified using Cell Culture Microplates (655090, Greiner Bio-one) in the Flex Station 3 plate reader (Molecular Devices), with measurements taken from the top at an excitation wavelength of 380 nm and an emission wavelength of 420 nm using the software SoftMax Pro (v7.2). The concentration of Cascade Blue that diffused to the basal compartment was calculated against a standard curve and the resulting apparent permeability (Papp) was quantified using the following formula:.

where Vbasal is the volume of the basal compartment, dCbasal is the measured concentration in the basal compartment, A is the area of the epithelial monolayer grown on the ECM (0.19477 cm2), dt is the time of the assay and Capical, t = 0 is the initial concentration added to the apical reservoir at the start of the assay. For infection experiments, one gentle DPBS wash was performed in the apical reservoir of control and infected samples to remove the majority of the grown biofilm before permeability assessment. The Cascade Blue, in addition to 200 µg ml−1 of gentamicin (G1397-10ML, Sigma-Aldrich), were supplemented in the chip medium. The assay was conducted over a period of 90 min, and fluorescence was measured from the bottom using a cell culture microplate that was covered with a transparent adhesive foil on top.

Recent findings suggest that the accumulation of mucus was facilitated by reducing the total apical volume from approximately 120 to 100 µl of chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to either approximately 30 µl or about 5 µl, based on the experimental needs. Generally, approximately 30 µl allowed for an accumulation of a less dense mucus that stayed hydrated. Accumulation with approximately 5 µl allowed for a denser layer of mucus that temporarily dried during the day and often acquired a yellow hue. The mucus accumulation strategy was initiated on day 4–5 of culture after full coverage of the ECM surface and appearance of goblet cells. The accumulation strategy was continued for 4–5 days and the accumulation of mucus on the epithelium surface was monitored by brightfield microscopy. To simulate liquid exchange, approximately 5 µl of fresh chip medium was added once or twice per day to compensate for liquid absorption by the intestinal epithelium and resulting air–liquid interface at the centre of the apical reservoir. In the accumulation with approximately 30 µl, the volume was monitored every day and adjusted to about 30 µl. The whole volume was exchanged every second day.

In a recent development, staining of the secreted mucus for live imaging was performed by an overnight incubation with 30 µl or 5 µl of 488 wheat germ agglutinin (25 µg ml−1; W11261, Invitrogen), respective of the accumulation strategy. In cases in which higher fluorescence signal of the secreted mucus was desired, additional wheat germ agglutinin incubations were performed in consecutive days. Shed cells were stained with an overnight incubation with SiR700 (3 µM; SC015, Sphirochrome) in chip medium. Confocal images were acquired as described in ‘Confocal microscopy imaging’. 3D reconstruction of the mucus was generated using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (4.6.1.27508) and adjusted for visualization purposes.

Recent findings suggest that for proteomic assessment of the luminal content, the mucus of the engineered intestines was accumulated for 5 days, reducing the luminal volume from approximately 100 µl to about 5 µl. In these samples, DMEM/ F12 (31331-028, Gibco) + HEPES (10 mM) + primocin (50 µg ml−1) was used as apical medium. For collection, the luminal content was collected by pipetting 5 µl of fresh apical medium up and down thoroughly and transferred to a Protein LoBind 1.5-ml tube (022431081, Eppendorf). This step was repeated a total of four times. The samples were immediately stored at −80 °C until further use.

Samples were processed into peptides using the iST kit (PreOmics), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Mass spectrometry analysis was conducted on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) device equipped with a Nanospray Flex Series Ion Source and a PRSO-V2 sonation oven (Sonation), which was coupled to an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Samples were resuspended in 2% acetonitrile and 0.5% formic acid in water and loaded onto a C18 trap column (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18 HPLC Columns 20 mm × 75 µm; 3 µm) at a flow rate of 20 μl min−1; peptides were separated using a 75-μm inner diameter C18 column (Aurora Column 25 cm × 75 µm C18 1.7 µm; Gen3; (IonOpticks). Chromatographic separation was achieved using the following conditions: buffer A was 0.1% formic acid in water; buffer B was 80% 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. The column oven and autosampler tray were held at 40 °C and 7 °C, respectively. The chromatographic gradient was run at a flow rate of 250 nl min−1 as follows: 0–47 min: linear gradient from 9 to 20% B; 47–90 min: linear gradient from 20 to 40% B; 90–92 min: linear gradient from 40 to 97%; 92 to 104 min: hold at 97%. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive mode with the spray voltage set to 1.7 kV and the ion transfer tube held at 275 °C (Xcalibur, v4.7 SP1). All measurements were performed in data-dependent mode. Precursor mass spectra were recorded in a range of 375–1,500 m/z with the resolution set at 240,000 the AGC (automatic gain control) target set in the standard mode and the maximum injection time in auto mode. For tandem mass spectrometry acquisition, data recorded in centroid mode with injection time was set to maximum 50 ms with a gain control setup at 100%. Normalized collision energy was set to 30. All experiments were recorded in ITMS mode and scan rate was turbo. Data were extracted and searched against the SwissProt database (June 2024) by using Proteome Discoverer 2.5 (Thermo Scientific) and Mascot (v2.8.2; Matrix Science). All cysteines were considered alkylated (carbamidomethyl), and oxidation of methionine and protein N-terminal acetylation were allowed as variable modifications. Data were first searched using fully tryptic constraints. Matched peptides were filtered using a percolator-based 1% false discovery rate. Intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) values were calculated with an in-house R script using R (v4.3.0), Biostrings (v2.68.1) and tidyverse (v2.0.0). In brief, the number of theoretically possible tryptic peptides with 6–30 amino acids was calculated based on an in silico tryptic digest of the human SwissProt database already used for the Proteome Discoverer (PD) search. The theoretical peptide count was then mapped to the PD output by protein accession. Finally, the iBAQ value was calculated by dividing the respective protein abundance by the theoretical number of tryptic peptides. Proteins with only one unique peptide and any missing values for any of the engineered intestine replicates within each donor were excluded from the analysis. iBAQ values for each protein were averaged first across engineered intestines within each donor and then across donors to generate the final iBAQ rank plots.

E. faecium (19434, American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)) inoculums were grown overnight at 230 rpm at 37 °C in 4 ml of brain heart infusion (1002417, MP Biomedicals) medium. L. rhamnosus (7469, ATCC) inoculums were grown overnight at 230 rpm at 37 °C at 5% CO2 and 95% humidity in 10 ml of De Man, Rogosa and Sharpe (MRS) medium (1106610500, Millipore). For both strains, 50-ml Mini Bioreactor tubes (431720, Corning) were used for the overnight cultures. Following overnight growth, the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) values of the cultures were measured to adjust the bacterial concentration to 108 CFU ml−1. The bacteria were then pelleted by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm (E. faecium) or 5,000 rpm (L. rhamnosus) for 1 min and washed once with PBS. Subsequently, the pellets were resuspended in 1 ml of DMEM, low glucose, pyruvate (31885-023, Gibco) + HEPES (1:100, 15630080, Gibco) medium and serially diluted. In the case of L. rhamnosus, a 10% (v/v) supplementation of MRS was added. Finally, the desired number of bacteria was added in 30 µl of the corresponding medium to the apical compartment of the engineered intestines, which were cultured in the absence of primocin since day 0. The co-cultures were maintained in the incubator until the end of the experiment. To measure the number of bacteria on the samples, the luminal content including mucus was pipetted up and down thoroughly and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube, capturing the predominant fraction of the apical reservoir. This step was repeated with extra 100 µl PBS washes. A serial dilution of the total collected content was performed and the bacteria were plated and counted in TSA plates (43019, Biomerieux).

Engineered intestines were cultured in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) without primocin until the day of infection. Different mucus accumulation strategies were followed depending on the condition (Mucushi: 4 days, 5 µl; Mucusint: 2 days, 5 µl; Mucuslo: 4 days, 120 µl + 1× wash before infection; see Fig. 3). The GFP reporter strain of S.Tm (14028GFP, ATCC) was used to infect the epithelial monolayer. S.Tm inoculums were grown overnight at 37 °C and 230 rpm in 10 ml of brain heart infusion (1002417, MP Biomedicals) medium with 100 µg ml−1 ampicillin (A53542, Sigma-Aldrich) using 50-ml Mini Bioreactor tubes (431720, Corning). Following overnight growth, the OD600 values of the cultures were measured and adjusted to desired concentration in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1). The desired number of bacteria (105 or 104 CFU according to the experiment) was added to the apical compartment on top of the epithelium and in a total volume of 5 µl to preserve the mucus structure. The co-culture was maintained in the incubator for 18 hpi or 24 hpi. To measure the number of bacteria on the samples, the luminal content was resuspended in 100 µl of PBS in situ, pipetted up and down thoroughly, and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube. This step was repeated one more time. Serial dilutions of the collected content were plated and counted in TSA plates (43019, Biomerieux). Gentamicin protection assays (see the next section) were performed to measure the number of intracellular bacteria.

Industry observers note that related to Figs. 3 and 5, engineered intestines in the absence of TRM cells were cultured in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) without primocin until the day of infection without mucus accumulation steps. Infections were carried out using provided WT and mutant strains (ΔfliC–ΔfljB, ΔsiiF, ΔinvG–ΔssaV, ΔssaV and ΔsteE) of S.Tm (strain 12023, NCTC; reference equivalent of ATCC 14028), either harbouring GFP-reporter plasmids or unlabelled, as specified in figure legends (Supplementary Table 1). For specific experiments, an additional S.Tm SL1344 WT and ΔinvG–ΔssrB strains were used (Supplementary Table 1). S.Tm inoculums were grown overnight at 37 °C and 200 rpm in 10 ml of LB medium (10855021, Gibco) with respective antibiotics using 50-ml Mini Bioreactor tubes. After that time, the inoculums were diluted 1:20 in invasion-inducing conditions56 (LB ± respective antibiotics + 0.3 M of NaCl (S/3161/60, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and incubated for 2.5 h (3 h for S.Tm SL1344 due to slower growth) at 37 °C and 250 rpm in 3 ml using 13-ml tubes in tilted position. Following growth, the OD600 values of the cultures were measured and adjusted to desired bacterial concentrations. Approximately 1.5 × 107 CFU (multiplicity of infection ~ 1:60) were added on the apical compartment resuspended in 50 µl of chip medium and incubated for 3 h in the incubator. Then, the apical bacteria were collected by two washes with 100 µl of PBS and either plated on TSA plates or discarded. Gentamicin protection assays were performed by adding fresh chip medium with 200 µg ml−1 of gentamicin (G1397, Sigma-Aldrich) apically and basally for 2 h, after which the concentration of gentamicin was reduced to 10 µg ml−1 and kept until the end of the experiment (total duration indicated as ‘hpi’) preserving the intracellular S.Tm population. Intracellular bacterial numbers were counted after one PBS wash, by collection of the epithelium with tweezers and subsequent lysis in a tube containing 100 µl of 0.5% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich). The content was incubated for 15 min and pipetted up and down at 0 min, 7 min and 15 min. A serial dilution of the lysate was plated in TSA plates.

In a recent development, experiments in the presence of TRM cells were carried out using immune chip medium without primocin (Supplementary Table 1) apically and basally. The same non-labelled S.Tm WT and mutant strains were used for infections. Infections were performed in the presence of 10 µg ml−1 of gentamicin basally to limit bacterial breach into the basal reservoir and direct S.Tm–TRM cell contact.

It has been revealed that to investigate the effect of oxidative stress on S.Tm intracellular replication, the small-molecule inhibitors ML385 (target NRF2, 20 µM; HY-100523, MedChemExpress), ASP-8731 (target BACH1, 20 µM; 4265, Tocris), IKE (target SLC7A11, 10 µM; S8877, Selleckchem), RSL3 (target GPX4, 2 µM; SML2234-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and the reactive oxygen species scavengers Fer-1 (15 µM donor 1 and 20 µM donor 2; S7243, Selleckchem) and liproxstatin-1 hydrochloride (3 µM donor 1 and 4 µM donor 2; 6113, R&D Systems) were added apically and basally at the start of the gentamicin treatment and kept for 24 h. DMSO was added to control samples apically and basally.

For investigation of TCR-dependent and TCR-independent IFNγ induction pathways, EpCAM–TCB (Roche) and small-molecule inhibitors were added to the basal reservoirs 4 h before S.Tm infection of the immunocompetent barriers: BIRB 796 (target p38 MAPK, 100 nM; 5989, Tocris); idelalisib 100 nM (target PI3K; 7631, Tocris); and LCK-5-IN (target LCK, 100 nM; HY-180888, MedChemExpress). To assess the effects of bacterial components, LPS (100 ng ml−1; L3024-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and flagellin (50 ng ml−1; tlrl-epstfla-5, InvivoGen) were introduced into the lumen of the immunocompetent barriers. These treatments were performed in parallel with S.Tm-infected epithelia, which served as infected controls, and were sustained until the end point of the experiment.

To analyse the cytokines in the supernatant of the engineered intestines, 100 µl supernatant was collected from both basal reservoirs per engineered intestine and pooled afterwards. Supernatants were quickly centrifuged to remove cell debris and frozen at −20 °C, followed by a transfer to −80 °C until further processing.

Recent findings suggest that assessment of the cytokines was performed using a custom-designed LEGENDplex panel (CXCL10, IL-8, sFas, BioLegend). Controls, standards and beads were prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were not diluted. In brief, 25 µl of the samples were mixed with 25 µl assay buffer and 25 µl mixed beads. The 25 µl diluted standard was mixed with 25 µl assay buffer and 25 µl mixed beads. Both samples and standard mixtures were dispensed in a V-bottom plate. Afterwards, samples were incubated for 2 h at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Samples were centrifuged at 500g for 2 min followed by removal of the supernatant. Samples were washed with 200 µl 1X wash buffer per well, followed by addition of 25 µl detection antibodies and incubation for 1 h at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Next, without washing, SA-PE was added and incubated for 30 min at room temperature on a shaker at 800 rpm. Samples were centrifuged at 500g for 2 min followed by removal of the supernatant to remove excess antibodies. Finally, 150 µl of 1X wash buffer was added before acquisition on Cytek Aurora with the 5 L configuration (Cytek) following the recommended experimental setup. To obtain absolute cytokine concentrations, the raw data were processed and analysed using the software provided by the manufacturer (LEGENDplex data analysis software, v2024-06-15, BioLegend).

Sources indicate that analyte concentrations were determined using a custom U-PLEX Immuno-Oncology Human Biomarker Group 1 Assay (Meso Scale Diagnostics (MSD)). The assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, U-PLEX plates were prepared by incubating linkers with their corresponding biotinylated capture antibodies for 30 min at room temperature, followed by overnight coating at 4 °C. Controls were reconstituted in assay diluent and standards were prepared via a sevenfold dilution; samples were diluted 1:5. Plates were washed, and either 25 µl of standard or 10 µl of sample (brought to a total volume of 50 µl with diluent) was added to each well. Plates were incubated for 2 h at room temperature with orbital shaking (500 rpm). Following a wash step, 50 µl of SULFO-TAG detection antibody solution was added per well and incubated for 2 h at room temperature (500 rpm). After a final wash, 150 µl of MSD GOLD read buffer was added, and the plates were immediately read using a MESO QuickPlex SQ 120 (or MESO Sector S 600) imager. Absolute cytokine concentrations were calculated using the MSD Discovery Workbench software (v4.0.13), accounting for the sample dilution. Samples under the limit of detection were set to 0.

Assessment of secreted cytokines from S.Tm WT and ΔinvG–ΔssaV strains was performed with the human cytokine 71-plex Discovery assay by the supplier. Samples below the limit of detection were not considered for analysis.

Sources indicate that the following microscopes were used for confocal imaging of the stained and live engineered intestines: (1) Nikon Ti2 microscope with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) equipped with a sCOMS camera (ORCA-Fusion BT, Hamamatsu Photonics). Depending on the application, the following objectives were used: ×4 proposal apo Lambda OFN25, ×10 plan apo Lambda OFN25 DIC N1, ×20 C S Plan Fluor LWD, ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2, ×25 C Sil plan apo Lambda S (Nikon Instruments). The extended depth-of-focus feature of the NIS-Elements software (v5.42.05, Nikon) was used to create focused brightfield and fluorescent images of the engineered intestines. In certain cases, images were further processed and colour adjusted using ImageJ software (2.3.0/1.54f). (2) Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope equipped with 3 power HyD detectors, white light laser (440–790 nm) using ×25 HC FLUOTAR L VISIR X25 objective (Leica Microsystems). Images were either visualized as maximum projection or 3D reconstructed using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (v4.6.1.27508).

In a recent development, 3D reconstructions of the epithelial layer with integrated TRM cells from the engineered intestinal whole-mount stainings were generated with the Imaris surface function (v9.9.1). Surfaces were rendered based on fluorescence intensities of the iCas9 CDH1–mScarlet3 reporter and CD3, and CD8 antibody stainings.

Recent findings suggest that proliferative cells were labelled using the Click-iT Plus EdU Alexa Fluor 488 Imaging Kit (C10637, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Engineered intestinal tissues were cultured as described above for 10 days. On day 10, EdU was added to the standard culture medium at a final concentration of 10 µM, and chips were returned to the incubator. After 2 h, one chip was fixed immediately in 4% PFA. The remaining two chips were washed three times with chip medium (Supplementary Table 1), with 2 h of incubation between washes, and returned to the incubator. One chip was fixed 2 days later, and the final chip was fixed after 4 days post-EdU pulse. After fixation, samples were washed in PBS and processed for EdU staining according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was performed using a Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope. Before immune cell seeding, TRM cells or T cells derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (isolation described above) were labelled with CellTrace Far Red (C34572, Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Afterwards, immuno-chips were prepared as described above. Timelapse imaging was performed 7–10 days (where indicated) post-co-culture setup with either a STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope with a ×25 HC FLUOTAR L VISIR X25 objective (Leica Microsystems) or with Nikon Ti2 microscope equipped with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) using with ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2 objective (Nikon Instruments). Images on Leica STELLARIS 8 were obtained in bidirectional mode with 1,024 × 1,024 pixels at 600 Hz. Images were acquired with varying Z-stack depth (z-steps, 4 µm). Samples were imaged between 42 and 60 min (where indicated). During imaging, samples were maintained in a microscopy incubation chamber at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (The Box, Life Imaging Services). For live imaging along the crypt–villus axis, engineered intestines were collected from the glass slide and cut in two followed by placing the engineered intestines perpendicularly on top of a glass dish. The engineered intestines were then fixated with a thin glass coverslip to avoid buoyancy due to medium in the dish. After acquisition, maximum-intensity projections were generated for downstream analysis.

Timelapse movies were analysed using CellProfiler. In brief, cells were segmented at each frame with multiotsu, morphological parameters were extracted and segmented cells were tracked over time using LAP algorithm with the following parameters: number of standard deviations for search radius = 80, search radius limits = 3–80 pixels, gap closing cost = 2, split alternative cost = 1, merge alternative cost = 1, mitosis alternative = 1, maximum gap displacement = 100 pixel, maximum split score = 10, maximum merge score = 5, maximal temporal gap = 6 and maximum mitosis distance = 40. The output per cell was analysed using KNIME (v5.2). The means and standard deviation of morphological features per track over time were calculated. The standard deviation of morphological features over time is a measure of the dynamism of cells as they use amoeboid motility. In addition, track lifetime and track total distance were calculated. Tracks with less than five frames were discarded.

Industry observers note that timelapse imaging of S.Tm intracellular replication was performed at 37 °C at 5% CO2 conditions with a Nikon Ti2 microscope equipped with CSU-W1 spinning disk (Yokogawa) using ×25 apo LWD 1.1 W DIC N2 objective (Nikon Instruments). Images were processed using ImageJ software (2.3.0/1.54f) and NIS-Elements software (Nikon).

Industry observers note that for fixed whole-mount staining and imaging, engineered intestines were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA in the chip slide. After 1 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three times with 1X DPBS. Engineered intestines were either stained in situ or collected using a biopsy puncher (3 mm in diameter) and transferred into a 24-well plate. Next, samples were permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich) in 1X DPBS for 2 h at room temperature on an orbital rocker at 50 rpm. Permeabilization was followed by a blocking step with blocking buffer (10% donkey serum (S30-M, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.01% Triton X-100 in DPBS 1X) for 4 h at room temperature on an orbital rocker or 16 h at 4 °C. Primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 1) were applied and incubated overnight at 4 °C on an orbital rocker. Afterwards, samples were washed three times for 1 h each at room temperature with 1X DBPS on an orbital rocker. Anti-species secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 1), DAPI (1 µg ml−1; 62249, Thermo Scientific) and phalloidin (Alexa Fluor 568 phalloidin A12380; Alexa Fluor 488 phalloidin A12379; Alexa Fluor 647 phalloidin A30107, Thermo Fisher Scientific) were incubated for 4 h at room temperature or 16 h at 4 °C on an orbital rocker, covering the sample with aluminum foil. Samples were washed three times for 1 h each with DPBS on an orbital rocker before imaging.

For engineered tissue, samples were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA in the chip slide. After 2 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three times before using a biopsy puncher (3 mm in diameter) to detach the ECM and tissue. In parallel, the engineered intestines histomold, specifically designed to facilitate co-planar embedding of up to 50 engineered intestines, was prepared as previously described8. In brief, liquid histogel was dispensed into the chip histomold and allowed to polymerize for 20 min at 4 °C. Following polymerization, the histoarray was demoulded. Engineered intestines were then transferred with a thin tweezer into the slits of the histoarray. After careful glueing of the engineered intestines in the wells of the histoarray (see Harter et al.8), the histoarray was completely filled and distributed into biopsy cassettes. Samples were dehydrated overnight using a vacuum filter processor (HistoCore PEARL, Leica). The following day, samples were embedded in liquid paraffin.

It has been revealed that for primary intestinal tissue, samples were washed three times in 1X DPBS and fixed in 4% PFA at room temperature. Fixation was performed for 24 h, although reduced to 3 h for smaller specimens to prevent over-fixation.

Sources indicate that the basal compartments of the engineered intestines were washed once with 1X DPBS before fixation with 4% PFA. The apical reservoir was neither washed nor fixed to preserve the integrity of the luminal content. After 2 h of fixation at room temperature, the engineered intestines were washed three more times only in the basal compartment. Next, the bottom glass of the chip slide was detached by applying mechanical pressure and the matrix was punched from the bottom of the hydrogel in upwards direction, keeping the epithelium and luminal content. The punched sample was then carefully covered with 8 µl of TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Finally, the sample was incubated for 15 min at 37 °C before the transfer to the slits of the histoarray, as described before.

Samples were dehydrated using a graded ethanol series as previously described8. In brief, tissues were held in 10% neutral buffered formalin for 5 min, followed by sequential dehydration steps: two washes in 70% ethanol (30 min each), one wash in 80% ethanol (1 h), and two washes in 96% ethanol (30 min each). Next, two steps of two 1-h incubations in 100% ethanol were performed, followed by two 45-min xylene baths. Finally, samples were held in paraffin until regular formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) setting.

According to recent reports, FFPE blocks were, unless otherwise specified, sectioned at a thickness of 3.5 µm and transferred on Superfrost Ultra Plus Gold Adhesion Slides. Slides were incubated in a slide oven overnight at 37 °C.

Recent findings suggest that H&E staining was executed in a fully automated manner following the standard protocol on a Ventana HE600 stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). AlcianBlue–PAS staining was performed fully automated using the AlcianBlue for PAS (860-003, Ventana) and PAS staining (860-014, Ventana) kits on the Ventana Benchmark (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). In brief, after three cycles of deparaffinization, slides were washed and 200 µl of PAS AlcianBlue incubated for 16 min at 37 °C. Wash was repeated, and 200 µl of PAS periodic acid was applied for 4 min, before another wash and 12 min of PAS Schiffs staining. Next, slides were washed again and 200 µl PAS neutralizer was added and incubated for 4 min. Finally, slides were washed with 100 µl before counterstaining the slide with 200 µl of PAS haematoxylin for 8 min. Afterwards, slides were coverslipped as indicated in the manufacturer’s instructions. H&E-stained, IHC and AlcianBlue–PAS-stained slides were imaged with a brightfield whole-slide scanner at ×40 (Hamamatsu, NanoZoomer, S360; pixel size of 0.23 µm per pixel) and viewed in NDP-view2 (v2.9.29).

According to recent reports, as previously described52, IHC staining of FFPE slides was performed using a Ventana Discovery Ultra automated tissue stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). The slides were baked for 8 min at 60 °C, followed by a deparaffinization cycle for 8 min at 69 °C (deparaffinization cycle repeated three times). Heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed with Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 7.8, CC1, 950-227, Ventana) at 95 °C for a total of 40 min. Depending on the host species of secondary antibody, the slide was incubated with either Discovery goat Ig block (760-6008, Ventana) or 10% donkey serum for 32 min at 37 °C followed by application of Discovery inhibitor (760-4840, Ventana) for 8 min. Afterwards, primary antibodies were applied (diluted in Discovery antibody diluent, 760-108, Ventana; for specific concentrations and incubation times, see Supplementary Table 1). Primary antibodies were detected using anti-species secondary antibodies conjugated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP; OmniMap anti-rabbit HRP (prediluted), 760-4311, Ventana; OmniMap anti-mouse HRP (prediluted), 760-4310, Ventana; OmniMap anti-rat HRP (prediluted), 760-4310, Ventana; and OmniMap anti-goat HRP, 760-4647, Ventana) for 16 min and visualized by conversion of 3,3′-diaminobenizidine (DAB; Discovery ChromoMap DAB kit, 760-159, Ventana). Samples were counterstained with haematoxylin (Haematoxylin II, 790-2208, Ventana) and blueing reagent (760-2037, Ventana). After dehydration with a standard series of alcohol (75%, 95%, 100% and 100% v/v; CAS64-17-5, Roche) followed by 100% xylol baths (444240050, ACROS Organoids), slides were coverslipped in the RCM7000 coverslipper (MEDITE) using a standard histology glue (00811-EX, Pertex). Slides were dried for at least 2 h before imaging.

According to recent reports, as previously described52, opal mIF staining of FFPE slides was performed using a Ventana Discovery Ultra automated tissue stainer (Roche Tissue Diagnostics). The slides were baked for 8 min at 60 °C, followed by a deparaffinization cycle for 8 min at 69 °C (deparaffinization cycle repeated three times). Heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed with Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 7.8, CC1, 950-227, Ventana) at 95 °C for a total of 40 min. Depending on the host species of secondary antibody, the slide was incubated with either Discovery goat Ig block (760-6008, Ventana) or 10% donkey serum for 32 min at 37 °C followed by application of Discovery inhibitor (760-4840, Ventana) for 8 min. Afterwards, primary antibodies were dispensed onto the slide (diluted in Discovery antibody diluent, 760-108, Ventana; for specific concentrations and incubation times, see Supplementary Table 1). Primary antibodies were detected using anti-species secondary antibodies conjugated with HRP (see above for catalogue numbers) for 16 min. Next, the corresponding opal dye (opal 480 FP150001KT, opal 520 FP1487001KT, opal 570 FP1488001KT, opal 620 FP1495001KT, opal 690 FP1497001KT and opal 780 FP1501001KT, Akoya Biosciences) were applied, previously prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. After each application of the primary antibody, followed by the corresponding secondary antibody and opal dye (with increasing fluorophore excitation wavelength), an antibody neutralization and denaturation step was applied to remove residual antibodies and HRP, before starting the staining cycle again with the Discovery inhibitor blocking step. Finally, samples were counterstained with DAPI (Roche). When used, fluorescein-labelled Jacalin (FL-1151-5, Vector Laboratories) was integrated into the mIF staining protocol by swapping it with the 520 opal dye and always applied last in the staining protocol.

As previously described52, opal mIF stainings were imaged and digitized using multispectral imaging of the Vectra Polaris (Perkin Elmer) using the MOTiF technology at ×20 magnification for all seven opal dyes (opal 480–780) and DAPI. Slides were imaged in a batch manner to ensure identical imaging settings and cross-comparability within each experiment for subsequent image analysis. Unmixing of channels and processing of images were performed with PhenoChart (v1.0.12) and inForm (v2.4). Images were processed as .qptiff tiles and fused in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). A pixel resolution of 0.5 µm per pixel was used.

High-resolution opal mIF images were obtained using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica) with a water-immersion objective (HC FLUOTAR L VISIR ×25/0.95 NA WATER). A white-light laser (440–790 nm) was used to image all opal dyes. Channel signals were acquired sequentially to reduce cross-bleeding. Images were obtained in bidirectional mode with 1,024 × 1,024 pixels (pixel size of 384.56 × 384.56 nm2) or 2,048 × 2,048 pixels (pixel size of 273.8 × 273.38 nm2). Images were either visualized as maximum projection or 3D reconstructed using the Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) software (v4.6.1.27508).

Image analysis of opal mIF images was performed with HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs) and HALO AI (v3.6.4134, Indica Labs). Sample annotation was either manually performed or by deploying the TMA module in HALO. For detection and annotation of the engineered intestines, a RandomForest (v2) classifier was used to distinguish organoids from background (for example, matrix; minimum object size more than 1,000 µm). Following validation, engineered intestines were handled as individual regions of interest (ROIs) and quantification was executed per ROI. The RandomForest (v2) classifier was integrated in the Area Quantification FL (v2.3.4) modules and used to quantify positive marker staining against either overall size of each individual object or normalized to the DAPI+ area of the object (as indicated in the figure legends) as well as for quantification of intensities. The HighPlex FL (v4.2.14) module was used to perform nuclear segmentation based on DAPI+ cells, assisted by HALO AI’s integrated ‘AI default nuclear segmentation type’) for phenotype analysis. The FISH-IF (v2.2.5) module was used to perform DAPI-based nuclear segmentation and identification of cells positive for single intracellular bacteria. Specific cell phenotypes were determined by colocalization of the respective markers of interest with the DAPI+ nuclei (including the cytoplasm radius (1.25 µm) and nuclear signals, depending on the marker of interest). By integrating the RandomForest (v2) or DenseNet (v2) classifier in the HighPlex analysis module, for example, localization of the T cells in the matrix or epithelium, was determined.

Assessment of the spatial patterning was performed by manually annotating the crypts and the top epithelial layer along the E-cadherin+ signal as separate ROIs. The basal side of the top epithelial layer served as the ROI border to the crypt underneath. Cell quantification was then performed within the separate annotations per engineered intestine using the Highplex FL module. Similarly, quantification of the thickness of mucus was performed by manually outlining two lines within the same annotation layer: one along the apical side of the E-cadherin+ epithelium of the top epithelial layer (excluding the crypt depth), and a second line along the lumen-facing top layer of the Jacalin+ mucus.

Positive controls on primary matched or non-matched primary intestinal tissue were included in every staining. In case of some experiments, negative controls were co-embedded within the same histoarray by experimental design, easing unbiased threshold adjustment and detection of potential unspecific antibody binding (for example, the epithelium-only control served as the negative control for immune markers; different intestinal regions within one FFPE block).

Recent findings suggest that quantification of the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine was performed with a RandomForest classifier (v2) in HALO (v3.6.4134.396, Indica Labs). Dozens of viable intestinal crypts from different donors were manually annotated using brightfield images of the engineered intestines acquired with the ×2 objective of the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope (11526227, Leica Microsystems). After brief verification, the algorithm was deployed to detect the number of viable crypts per engineered intestine. All brightfield images were acquired with the Leica Dmi1 inverted microscope with ×2, ×4 and ×10 objectives.

Industry observers note that statistical analysis was carried out with GraphPad Prism (v10.6.1; GraphPad software). The number of donors is indicated as ‘d = x’, whereas the number of independent engineered intestines within each donor is referred to as ‘n = x’ in the respective figure legend. The number of repeated independent experiments is indicated as ‘e = x’. Data normality was evaluated with Shapiro–Wilk normality test and Q–Q plots. When comparing two sets of data, paired or unpaired two-tailed t-tests were carried out, including Welch’s correction when the standard deviation determined not identical between the groups by a F-test. In case the data were not normally distributed, Mann–Whitney sum-rank tests were performed. For comparisons involving more than two datasets and multiple variables, we performed one-way and two-way ANOVA, including Tukey’s, Dunnett’s or Šídák’s multiple comparisons test comparisons when comparing to a control condition. Nested one-way ANOVA was performed when d < 3, comparing the data across the number of independent engineered intestines (n). A Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparison test was performed instead of one-way ANOVA when the data did not follow normal distribution. Data were visualized with their mean and standard deviation, with the exact P values highlighting the statistical significance in the respective figure legend.

Before dissociation, surfaces were cleaned with RNase AWAY Decontamination Reagent (10328011, Invitrogen) and all tubes were coated with a coating solution containing HBSS −Ca2+/−Mg2+ (14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec) at 4 °C for at least 15 min. Multiple engineered intestines were pooled for each scRNA-seq and scMultiome, as indicated in the figure legends. Intestinal monolayers were detached from the matrix, collected and transferred to DNA LoBind 1.5-ml tubes (22431021, Eppendorf) with 1 ml of coating solution using forceps. In the case of the scMultiome experiment, where the epithelium integrity was compromised, the epithelium and hydrogel matrix were apically punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube. The punched hydrogel was dissolved by incubating the mix with 1 ml of collagenase type I (100 U ml−1; 17100017, Gibco) in Advanced DMEM/F12 for 15 min at 37 °C, following three washing steps in coating solution to clean the presence of collagenase in the sample and remove the digested hydrogel. Pooled and cleaned monolayers were pipetted up and down 50 times to mechanically disrupt the monolayers into smaller fragments. The single-cell dissociation was performed using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (130-092-628, Miltenyi Biotec). In brief, the samples were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was removed and the samples were incubated with 1 ml of the enzymeP Mix 1 at 37 °C for a total of 15 min, homogenizing the sample every 5 min by pipetting up and down a total of 50 times with a P1000 tip. After the first incubation, 30 µl of enzyme A Mix2 was added to the sample and incubated for 10 min, with homogenization steps every 5 min and inspection of the suspension under a brightfield microscope. The single-cell suspension was filtered through a PluriStrainer Mini 40 µm (43-10040-40, Pluriselect), previously coated with coating solution, into new 1.5-ml DNA LoBind tubes and centrifuged at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C.

Sources indicate that for scRNA-seq or scMultiome experiments, the pellets were washed a total of three times with coating solution at 450g for 5 min at 4 °C. Next, the samples were counted using the Countless 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Invitrogen) and adjusted to the desired concentrations for multiplexing, nuclei isolation or loading on the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

According to recent reports, for flow cytometry, FACS and Imagestream experiments, the pellets were washed 1× in DPBS before incubation with eBioscience Fixable Viability Dye eFluor 780 (1:2,000; 65-0865-14, Thermo Scientific) + TruStain FcX (1:200; 422301, BioLegend) in DPBS for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Next, the samples were spinned down, resuspended in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS), and incubated with PE-EpCAM (1:100; 324206, BioLegend) for 5 min at 4 °C in dark conditions. Single stained and unstained controls were prepared in parallel for compensation. After FACS, the sorted cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted before loading on the Chromium X.

According to recent reports, cell suspensions were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min at 4 °C before filtering through 70-µm strainers. For flow cytometric quantification of S.TmGFP-infected cells, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 250 µl of FACS buffer and analysed using a five-laser Cytek Aurora spectral flow cytometer. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software, and quantification of GFP+ cell fractions was performed in FlowJo (v10; BD Biosciences).

For FACS, fully stained, single stained and unstained samples were resuspended in 150 µl of FACS buffer. Bulk GFP+ and GFP− populations were isolated using a five-laser Cytek Aurora CS spectral cell sorter equipped with a 100-µm nozzle. Spectral unmixing with autofluorescence extraction was performed using Cytek Spectroflo CS software. Target cell populations were collected into low protein-binding 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes (Eppendorf). Next, the cells were centrifuged, resuspended in FACS buffer and counted for scRNA-seq on the Chromium X.

It has been revealed that for single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), single cells were index sorted using a five-laser BD FACSAria Fusion with a 100-µm nozzle into individual wells of a 384-well plate filled with lysis buffer (Single Cell Discoveries). Cells were grouped and sorted by GFP level (GFP−, GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi) to ensure equal representation in the final dataset of each group. Following sorting, plates were immediately stored at −80 °C until library preparation. Additional cells were also sorted into a lysis buffer containing 0.5% Triton X-100 (T8787, Sigma-Aldrich) for CFU counting within the same experiment.

Sources indicate that sorted GFP+ and GFP− cells were concentrated by centrifugation and resuspended in 25 µl of FACS buffer for analysis using a four-laser Cytek Amnis ImagestremX MKII dual CCD camera imaging flow cytometer. The 488-nm and 642-nm excitation lasers were set to a power of 10 mW and 150 mW, respectively, and data were acquired using the ×60 objective. Brightfield images were collected in channels 1 and 9, whereas fluorescence signals for GFP, EpCAM-PE and eFluor-780 were detected in channels 2, 3 and 12, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that imageStream data were analysed using IDEAS (v6.4.9.0). For each dataset, a compensation matrix was generated using the single-colour controls and the software compensation wizard, and applied to the relevant dataset. Events were gated to only keep contrasted, unclipped, EpCAM+GFP+ images of single host cells. The IDEAS internalization tool (GFP) was used to filter for host cells displaying intracellular GFP signal from the analysis and to quantify the prevalence of bacterial internalization. To perform spot counting in host cells, another filtering step to discard unfocused GFP signal was performed. With this filtering in place, we could start performing GFP spot counting using a series of machine learning classifiers. This was performed using IDEAS machine learning functionality. First, we manually selected two mutually exclusive populations of cells: 25 cells displaying a single GFP colony, 25 cells showing 2 or more than 2 colonies. A first machine learning classifier was trained on these two populations, and subsequently used to classify cells in two categories: ‘one colony’ and ‘more than one colony’. From the more-than-one-colony pool of events, the same strategy was used to train a second machine learning model on two mutually exclusive populations: 25 cells displaying 2 colonies, and 25 cells displaying more than 2 colonies. The model was run on the more than one colony data to classify cells in two fresh categories: two colonies versus more than two colonies. The obtained mutually exclusive populations were manually curated to fix misclassification of a few events. Cells belonging to the more-than-two-colonies population were manually classified into further populations: ‘three colonies’ and ‘more than three colonies’. Of note, the features weighting the most in our two machine learning classifiers were related to the area and ellipse-fitting parameters of the GFP signal displayed by the colonies.
