In a recent development, after collection of the epithelium using forceps, the remaining matrix and TRM cells were punched using a 3-mm puncher and transferred to a 1.5-ml tube containing warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1). Samples were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. After incubation, the sample was centrifuged at 500g for 2 min at 4 °C and washed with 1 ml of HBSS (−Ca2+ or −Mg2+; 14175095, Gibco) + 1% BSA (130-091-376, Miltenyi Biotec). This step was repeated twice. Before final cell counting, the Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions to remove apoptotic cells and then passed through a 40-µm Flowmi filter (BAH136800040, Millipore Sigma). Afterwards, the TRM cells were transferred to a 0.5-ml tube to facilitate visualization and accurate cell counting using the Countless 3 FL before loading into the Chromium X (10X Genomics).

Nuclei isolation was performed based on 10X Genomics demonstrated protocol CG000365 rev C. In brief, single cells were centrifuged for 4 min at 400g and 4 °C. The cell pellet was resuspended in cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20, 0.1% Nonidet P40 substitute, 0.01% digitonin and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor). After 6 min on ice, cold wash buffer was added (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl2, 1% BSA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Tween-20 and 1 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor) and nuclei were spun for 5 min at 500g and 4 °C. The pellet was resuspended in cold wash buffer and nuclei were counted with propidium iodide (ViaStain AO/PI, CS2-0106-5ML, Nexcelom Bioscience) using the Countess 3 FL (AMQAF2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific). After spinning, nuclei were resuspended in diluted nuclei buffer (10X Genomics) at recommended concentrations for 10X Genomics scMultiome. The quality of isolated nuclei was evaluated by microscopy with DAPI and brightfield.

Single-cell RNA-seq libraries were generated using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ (v3.1) reagents according to user manual CG000315 rev E. For multiplexed scRNA-seq, single-cell suspensions of nine biological samples were individually tagged with 10X Genomics 3′ CellPlex Set A reagents according to the demonstrated protocol CG000391 rev B protocol 1. Equal amounts of tagged cells were pooled together for each sample. Three lanes of Chromium Next GEM Chip G were loaded targeting 30,000 cells per lane. Cell encapsulation and library preparation were performed according to user guide Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kits (v3.1) with Feature Barcode technology for cell multiplexing CG000388 rev C. Single-nucleus multiome was performed using 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression reagents and corresponding user guide CG000338 rev F. Two lanes were loaded per sample targeting 10,000 cells per lane. All single-cell libraries (scRNA, single-nucleus RNA, Multiplex and single-nucleus ATAC) were quantified with Qubit 1X dsDNA HS (Q33231, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Kit (5067-4626, Agilent Technologies) and were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X Plus platforms.

For total single-cell total RNA-seq (VASA-seq), libraries were generated by Single Cell Discoveries, with the inclusion of a depletion step targeting the S.Tm 5S, 16S and 23S rRNAs. Libraries were sequenced aiming for a target coverage of 300,000 raw reads per cell.

According to recent reports, we ran Cell Ranger (v8.0.0) multi-pipeline with 10X Genomics References 2024-A (hg38, GENCODE v44) as reference for read alignment, demultiplexing and gene quantification of multiplexed scRNA-seq data; Cell Ranger (v7.1.0) for scRNA-seq data of TRM cells; Cell Ranger (v9.0.1) for scRNA-seq data from FACS-sorted epithelium after infections with S.Tm WT and mutants (hereafter referred as ‘sorted infection dataset’); and Cell Ranger Arc (v2.0.1) with 10X Genomics References 2020-A (hg38, GENCODE v32) for scMultiome data. We then loaded the Cell Ranger and Cell Ranger Arc pipelines filtered count matrix to Seurat (v4.3.0.1)77 and Signac (v1.10.0)78 for further preprocessing.

It has been revealed that for the multiplexed scRNA-seq data of engineered epithelium, cells with fewer than 500 or more than 6,000 genes expressed, or total unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts exceeding 30,000, or mitochondrial gene percentage above 25% were removed. For the TRM cell data, we only retained cells with more than 500 genes, UMI counts between 1,000 and e10 and mitochondrial percentage less than 15%. For the epithelial data with and without TRM cell co-culture, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, UMI counts between 3,000 and 50,000 and mitochondrial percentage less than 25%. For the sorted infection dataset, we only retained cells with more than 1,000 genes, less than 30,000 UMI and mitochondrial percentage less than 50%.

Sources indicate that for all datasets, raw counts were normalized using the ‘NormalizeData’ function with a scale factor of 10,000. Three thousand highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using the variance-stabilizing transformation (‘vst’) method. Data were scaled and principal component analysis was performed using these variable features. The first 20 principal components were used as input for ‘FindNeighbors’ and dimensional reduction with UMAP. The resulting graph was used for ‘FindClusters’ with the Louvain algorithm at resolution 1.0.

Recent findings suggest that for the multiplexed data, after inspection of regional marker gene expression, we excluded the potential foregut sample (‘don55’) marked by SOX2 and a sample with mixed ileal and colonic identity (‘IF17ile’, FABP6+ and SATB2+). We then removed ribosomal genes, mitochondrial genes, genes located on sex chromosomes and genes without proper gene symbols to avoid influence of these confounding factors to the integration of this dataset derived from multiple donors and reran the pipelines from normalization to clustering.

Epithelial cell-type annotation was initialized on cluster level based on expression of canonical intestinal cell type and regional markers, including: stem cells (LGR5, OLFM4, SMOC2 and ASCL2), absorptive cells (APOA4, FABP6 and CEACAM7), goblet cells (MUC2 and FCGBP), enteroendocrine cells (CHGA), transit-amplifying cells (MKI67), BEST4+ cells (BEST4), epithelial regional identity markers (SATB2, GATA4, CDX2 and PDX1) and leukocytes (PTPRC). Clusters with similar expression patterns were merged and resulted in a coarse-grained annotation. Differential features between proximal, distal and colonic enterocytes and colonocytes were derived from the top 500 marker genes using the ‘wilcoxauc’ function of the ‘presto’ R package on normalized RNA expression values (Wilcoxon test, logFC > log(1.1), adjusted P < 0.05). Enrichment for ‘BP’ (biological process) and ‘MF’ (molecular function) Gene Ontology was performed with the function enrichGO from the clusterProfiler package. Detected genes were used as background and all terms in the org.Hs.eg.db database were used. The enrichment score for each term was calculated by subtracting the significant −log10-transformed hypergeometric test Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected P value of the region of interest and the average of those from the other two regions. Missing values or not undefined numeric results for one region were set to the minimum of the other two regions for visualization.

Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) subtype annotation was performed following subclustering. Subtype-specific signatures (‘EC’: TPH1; ‘MX’: GHRL and MLN; ‘K’: GIP; ‘L’: PYY and GCG; ‘D’: SST; ‘I’: CCK; and ‘Prog’: NEUROG3) were calculated using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat on normalized RNA expression values. Cells were assigned to the identity with the highest score, provided the score exceeded a minimum threshold (0.1). Cells that did not meet this criteria were categorized as ‘EEC unassigned’.

According to recent reports, for the multiplexed data and the sorted infection dataset, which did not resolve a cluster representing distal small intestine stem cells, we extracted stem cells from the continuum to absorptive cells based on summarized expression levels of stem cell marker genes. For the multiplexed data, we selected the top ten genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5, SMOC2 and ASCL2 across stem cells and absorptive cells and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 60th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as absorptive cells. To reduce the noise of classification solely based on scores of individual cells, we performed high-resolution clustering (resolution = 5), and defined cells belonging to the high-resolution clusters with more stem cells than absorptive cells were defined as stem cells, regardless of their individual scores. For the sorted infection dataset, we subsetted two initial clusters (resolution = 1 from the whole dataset) with LGR5+ cells. We selected the top five genes with the highest correlation with summarized scaled expression of LGR5 and SMOC2 across stem cells and colonocytes and calculated the stem cell score of each cell by summing the scaled expression of selected genes. We defined cells with stem cell scores higher than the 90th percentile of positive scores as stem cells and others as colonocytes. The distribution of the manually extracted stem cells fits the visual inspection on the LGR5 feature plot. For the colonocyte-subtype annotation in the sorted infection dataset, colonocyte clusters with more than 80% cells from the GFP+ samples were collectively defined as ‘enriched in GFP+’, the colonocyte cluster with less than 0.1% cells from the non-infected sample were defined as ‘depleted in non-infected’, and other colonocyte clusters were defined as ‘shared’.

Industry observers note that to resolve the goblet cell heterogeneity in the multiplexed data, we subsetted goblet cells from the entire dataset based on their coarse-grained cell-type annotation. The subset was re-normalized, and variable features were recalculated and reclustered (resolution = 1). We excluded clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 to get non-proliferative goblet cells and performed subclustering. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function implemented by the presto package and defined significant cluster markers with Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference (pct_in) > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1.

TRM cell-type annotation was performed on the cluster level. We first annotated epithelial cells (EPCAM+), B cells (CD79B+) and proliferative CD4+ T cells (MKI67+), then annotated non-proliferative T cell subtypes based on mapping to a public adult human intestine tissue immune cell reference with two complementary approaches. We identified cell-type markers of the in vitro and tissue data separately using the wilcoxauc function with cut-off Wilcoxon rank-sum test Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05, expressed cell percentage difference > 10%, expression logFC > 0.1. We quantified the marker gene overlap significance between in vitro and tissue cell types using −log10-transformed Fisher’s two-sided exact test nominal P value. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types with the strongest overlap, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 10. In parallel, we calculated Spearman correlation between our in vitro and tissue cell types based on the markers defined in both systems. For each in vitro cell type, we got the top three tissue cell types showing the highest transcription program similarity, or the subset of top three if the significance difference between pairs of top three was larger than 0.1. We then annotated the in vitro T cells as the overlap of overlap-based and similarity-based matched tissue cell types. On the basis of further inspection of individual canonical marker gene expression, we manually renamed activated CD4 T, activated CD8 T and MAIT-like CD4 as CD4 TRM, CD8 TRM and CD4 TRMTH17, respectively.

According to recent reports, to construct an adult human intestine tissue transcriptome reference, we collected the count matrix and cell-type annotation of epithelial cells from three public adult intestine multi-region scRNA-seq datasets79,80,81. All datasets were processed using Seurat (v4). After merging the datasets, we performed LogNormalize normalization with a scale factor of 10,000. We identified HVGs independently for each dataset using the vst method, selecting 3,000 HVGs per dataset. We then selected integration features across datasets using the SelectIntegrationFeatures function. We ran principal component analysis using the selected integration features and retrieved the top 50 principal components. We integrated the data with Cluster Similarity Spectrum (CSS)82 stratified by sample, and default setting for other parameters. We performed dimension reduction with UMAP, and Louvain clustering based on CSS embeddings using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions at a resolution of 1.0. We compared the data without batch effect correction, integration with Harmony or with CSS integration, and chose CSS-integrated results based on visual inspection of canonical cell-type marker gene expression.

According to recent reports, to establish a consistent cell-type annotation scheme across datasets, we created a mapping between original annotations and standardized categories. We classified cells into major epithelial lineages: absorptive cells (enterocytes and colonocytes), goblet cells, BEST4+ cells, EECs, follicle-associated epithelium, stem cells, M cells, Paneth cells, secretory progenitors and tuft cells. We further refined these annotations by incorporating regional information. We defined the G2M-phased cells defined by the CellCycleScoring function in Seurat within the clusters with enriched expression of MKI67 as the transit-amplifying cells. Cell-type identities were validated using established marker genes. For rare cell populations (for example, Paneth cells and tuft cells), we calculated expression-based scores using canonical markers (DEFA5 and DEFA6 for Paneth cells; RGS13, AVIL and ALOX5 for tuft cells) and assigned cells based on these scores. To be more specific, we identified the top five positively correlated genes with summarized DEFA5 and DEFA6 scaled expression profiles across epithelium among the 3,000 HVGs as feature genes of Paneth cells. We summed up the scaled expression levels of the selected top five Paneth-associated genes for each cell as the Paneth cell feature score, and defined cells with scores exceeding 97.5th percentile of all positive scores as Paneth cells. We applied a similar procedure to identify tuft cells, with 10 tuft cell feature genes and using 95 percentile as the selection cut-off.

To establish a tissue reference for colonocyte subtype annotation in the Salmonella dataset, we subsetted to non-small intestine transit-amplifying cells, stem cells and colonocytes, integrated the data with CSS and performed subclustering based on the CSS embeddings at resolution = 0.4. We identified cluster markers using the wilcoxauc function in the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We selected the top 100 markers ranked by logFC from each cluster and unified them as features for comparison between in vitro and tissue colonic stem cells and colonocytes.

To further reconstruct the differentiation trajectory from stem cells to colonocytes in primary tissues (excluding transit-amplifying cells), we computed a diffusion map using the DiffusionMap function in the destiny package on the CSS space and we defined the rank of the first diffusion component (DC1) as the inferred differentiation pseudotime. We ordered the cells along the pseudotime, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. We calculated the Pearson correlation coefficients between the bin average expression levels and the bin order for each gene. The 50 genes with the strongest positive correlations were selected as pseudotime-positive correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in mature colonocytes, and the 50 genes with the strongest negative correlations as pseudotime-negative correlating genes, which show higher expression levels in stem cells and early colonocytes. We then applied these tissue-derived differentiation-related genes on the sorted infection dataset. We used the AddModuleScore function in Seurat based on normalized RNA expression values of the pseudotime positively and negatively correlating genes separately. A composite differentiation score of the cells in the chip was defined as the difference between the positive and negative module scores. We ordered the colonocytes according to the differentiation score from premature to mature, partitioned them into 25 bins and calculated the average gene expression of each bin. The obtained bin average gene expression profiles are defined as expression profiles along the reconstructed pre-mature-to-mature colonocyte differentiation trajectory.

To create a unified peak list across samples, we called open chromatin-accessible regions in each sample using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1) with the CallPeaks function and then quantified them with FeatureMatrix in Signac. We only kept regions located on standard chromosomes. We annotated peaks to most nearby genes using the annotatePeak function in ChIPseeker based on the Ensemble (v98) annotation. We only retained cells with ATAC UMI count between 200 and 50,000, RNA UMI count less than 20,000, RNA gene number between 500 and 5,000, mitochondrial percentage less than 50%, nucleosome signal (calculated by NucleosomeSignal) less than 1, transcription start site enrichment score (calculated by TSSEnrichment) less than 1 and hg38 genome blacklist ratio less than 0.5%. We ran the same pipeline of scRNA-seq data from read count normalization to dimension reduction and clustering as described in the previous section (‘Preprocessing and cell-type annotation of scRNA-seq data’). For the scATAC-seq data, we performed term frequency-inverse document frequency normalization on read counts using the RunTFIDF function. We defined the regions with over 1% detection rate as top features and RunSVD based on the top features. We projected cells into two-dimension UMAP embeddings and FindNeighbors based on top 2–50 latent semantic indexing.

We performed major epithelial cell-type annotation on RNA cluster level based on canonical cell-type marker expression. We subsetted to colonic stem cell and colonocyte clusters, calculated the Spearman correlation coefficients between in vitro and tissue stem cell to colonocyte clusters using the in vitro-expressed colonic stem cell and colonocyte feature genes defined in the tissue reference. We performed hierarchical clustering on the in vitro clusters based on the similarity profiles and classified them into stem cells and four colonocyte subtypes indicating differential maturity accordingly. Colonocyte clusters with mostly exclusive presence in the Salmonella-infected sample were defined as infection-specific colonocyte clusters. We transferred RNA-level cell-type annotations to ATAC data, and merged subtypes that could not be clearly resolved by ATAC data as annotations on the ATAC level.

Sources indicate that we performed differential analysis for co-clustered S.Tm infection and control cells in each cluster of stem cells, colonocytes and goblet cells, which have sufficient cell numbers for robust estimation. For infection-specific clusters, which have less than 20 control cells in the clusters, we first identified matched control sample cells for each infected sample cell using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 in the top 20 principal component space. We identified DEGs between matched control and infected cells using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1. We applied the same procedure to identify DEGs in the epithelium induced by TRM cell co-culture except that we did not need to use the k-nearest neighbour search approach to get matched control cells as there was no condition-specific cluster.

It has been revealed that to identify DARs between Salmonella-infected and control conditions, we implemented a statistical framework based on linear regression modelling of binarized chromatin accessibility data, with sequencing depth (UMI counts) as covariate. Specifically, for each open chromatin region i, we fitted:.

Null model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts, family = binomial).

Full model: glm(e ~ UMIcounts + condition, family = binomial).

where e represents the binarized accessibility state vector for region i across all cells. We applied a Chi-squared test comparing the two models using ANOVA. Regions were considered differentially accessible if they had Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 and highlighted at least a 0.5% difference in the proportion of cells with the region accessible between Salmonella-infected and control conditions.

We reconstructed the gene regulatory networks from the scMultiome data along the stem-cell-to-coloncyte trajectory and each of the stem cell, colonocyte and goblet cell types shared by both control and infection conditions using Pando83 separately. We used the infection-induced DEGs and 5,000 HVGs of each data as input HVGs for Pando. We constrained our candidate regulatory regions to be either conserved in mammals (defined in phastConsElements20Mammals.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando) or overlapped with ENCODE regions (defined in SCREEN.ccRE.UCSC.hg38 provided by Pando), and showing significantly correlated profiles with HVGs as output by LinkPeaks in Signac at the default distance threshold of 500 kb. We ran find_motifs and used the Pando-provided transcription factor-binding site (TFBS) motif database compiled from JASPAR and CIS-BP as reference for Pando to identify TFBS in candidate regulatory regions. We ran the infer_grn function with a Gaussian generalized linear model (model = ‘glm’) to infer regulatory coefficients from log-normalized transcript counts and binarized peak counts summarized to SLM algorithm-defined ATAC clusters (resolution = 10). We identified transcription factor–target gene modules using the find_modules function with default settings. We combined the modules from different datasets as inferred transcription factor–target pairs.

Recent findings suggest that for visualization, we selected the condition-dependent DEGs with the top 500 absolute value of expression log-transformed fold change between conditions and the union set of the top three-correlated Pando-predicted transcription factors of each selected DEGs. We calculated pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients of expression profiles across cell types and conditions between selected genes, reduced the dimension of obtained correlation matrix to 20 principal components using prcomp_irlba in the irlba package and further projected genes to two-dimension embeddings using umap in the uwot package with the obtained principal components as input.

In a recent development, we ran the AddMotifs function in Signac to add the TFBS motifs information on our detected open chromatin regions and obtained a motif occurrence matrix. To identify TFBS motifs over-represented in open chromatin regions with increased accessibility upon infection in each cell type, we ran FindMotifs in Signac on the top 200 upregulated accessible regions, with 30,000 open chromatin regions with matched overall GC content retrieved by the MatchRegionStats function as background.

We defined three comparisons to characterize the luminal effects: (1) ΔSPI-1/2 non-invaded (ΔSPI-1/2Out, GFP−) versus non-infected, (2) WT non-invaded (WTOut, GFP−) versus non-infected, and (3) WTOut versus ΔSPI-1/2Out; and three for intracellular effects: (1) WT invaded (WTIn, GFP+) versus WTOut, (2) ΔsteE invaded (ΔsteEIn, GFP+) versus WTIn, and (3) ΔSPI-2In versus WTIn. We subsetted to colonocytes. Genes detected in at least 50 colonocytes were retained, excluding features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ‘ENSG’. Pairwise comparisons were conducted between predefined experimental conditions within each colonocyte cluster. Comparisons were performed only when at least 20 cells were available in at least one condition. When one of the conditions contained fewer than 20 cells, we supplemented with cells from other clusters of the same condition that were defined as nearest neighbours of the other condition, using get.knnx of the FNN package with k = 1 based on Euclidean distance in the top 20 principal component space. Differential expression testing was performed using the wilcoxauc function of the presto R package on normalized RNA expression values. We identified DEGs between conditions per cluster using the wilcoxauc function by the presto package, with cut-offs adjusted P < 0.05, pct_in > 10 and logFC > 0.1.

We then pooled genes defined as significant DEGs in at least one comparison in at least one cluster as the union set of condition DEGs. We then calculated the colonocyte average expression levels of each condition. We calculated the expression difference between WTOut and non-infected—namely, diff_WT_vs_NI, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTOut versus non-infected—and between WTIn and WTOut—namely, diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT, where positive values indicate upregulation in WTIn versus WTOut. We ranked the gene according to diff_WT_vs_NI, took the top 50 genes as feature genes and used the AddModuleScore function to calculate the luminal effect gene module score, and applied the same procedure for diff_WT_GFP_vs_WT values for intracellular effect gene module score.

We used CellChat (v2)84 to infer intracellular communications between co-cultured intestinal epithelial cells and TRM cells. Normalized expression data were extracted from the epithelium and TRM cell combined Seurat RNA assay, and cell-type labels were used to group cells for interaction analysis. We used the built-in human CellChatDB database as reference for ligand–receptor interactions. To reduce computational cost, we subsetted the expression data to include only signalling genes present in the database. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified using the identifyOverExpressedGenes and identifyOverExpressedInteractions functions. Communication probabilities were computed using the computeCommunProb function with type = truncatedMean and trim = 0.05. We subsetted to interactions between proximal small intestinal enterocytes and immune cell types, excluding proliferating CD4+ T cells for visualization.

Read alignment, gene expression quantification and cell filtering of the VASA-seq data were performed by Single Cell Discoveries. In brief, raw sequencing data were processed using Cutadapt (v4.9) to remove adapter sequences and homopolymers, followed by Ribodetector (v0.3.1) to filter out ribosomal reads. Processed reads were then aligned to the reference genome using STARsolo (v2.7.11b), with the parameter–soloFeatures set to GeneFull_Ex50pAS. The human reference genome used was GRCh38, ENSEMBL release 103. The S.Tm reference genome was downloaded from EnsemblBacteria Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium str. 14028S str. LT2 14028S (GCA_000022165) release 62. The resulting single-cell-level gene count matrices were used as inputs for downstream analysis in R.

Sources indicate that to improve the gene annotation for the S.Tm genome, we performed sequence alignment for the genes in the S.Tm strain 14028S annotation against the S.Tm strain 14028 annotation (GCF_028596185.1_ASM2859618v1). Out of the 1,542 genes with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 242 were mapped to annotated genes with common names in the S.Tm 14028 annotation by blastn85,86 with more than 90% of sequence similarity.

Sources indicate that cells without GFP signal, UMI count of less than 3,500 or External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) counts of less than 450 were excluded. Raw counts were normalized using the NormalizeData function in Seurat with a scale factor of 10,000.

It has been revealed that according to FACS index sorting values, cells with GFP < 500 were defined as GFP−, 500 or more and less than 2,000 as GFPlo, 2,000 or more and 10,000 or less as GFPint, and more than 10,000 as GFPhi. For human genes, only genes detected in at least 10% of cells in at least one GFP signal group were included in the differentially expressed test. For each retained gene, expression was modelled using two nested linear models. The reduced model included log-transformed total UMI counts per cell and the percentage of mitochondrial reads as technical covariates, whereas the full model additionally included the GFP signal group as a factor. The contribution of the GFP signal group was assessed by ANOVA comparing the full and reduced models. Genes with Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. To assign directionality, we calculated the difference in average expression between the GFPhi and GFPlo groups and assigned the directionality accordingly.

In a recent development, for S.Tm, we applied the same differentially expressed test strategy, but only included GFP+ cells for comparison. Given the sparsity of the bacteria transcripts, we reduced the detection rate cut-off to 1%. After further excluding ERCC transcripts and features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 3,137 genes were left as input for the differentially expressed test. We used nominal P < 0.05 as the cut-off to get marginally significant bacterial DEG.

R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., M.N., N.G. and J.G.C. conceived the study. R.L.-S., M.F.H., Q.Y., N.G. and J.G.C. wrote the manuscript. M.N. designed and fabricated the fluidic device and crypt stamps, with support from J.A. and S.M. M.P.L. contributed to the development of the fluidic device holding the tissues. M.N. and R.L.-S. generated the artwork design. M.F.H. and R.L.-S. designed and performed most of the experiments in the article. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.N., N.A. and J.B. optimized the epithelium growth conditions. M.F.H. isolated the organoid lines and TRM cells from primary tissue. R.L.-S., M.F.H., M.A.-B., L.G.-T. and S.S. performed scRNA-seq, scMultiome and VASA-seq experiments. M.A.-B. and L.G.-T. generated the sequencing libraries. Q.Y. performed the computational analysis of scRNA-seq and scMultiome data, with support and data interpretation from R.L.-S., S.S. and M.F.H. M.F.H., R.L.-S. and J.A. co-developed the histomold. I.C. and S.T. performed the FFPE processing, sectioning, H&E and AlcianBlue–PAS stainings, with support from M.F.H. M.F.H. performed the immunohistochemistry and mIF stainings, imaging and analysis with support from R.L.-S. and M.N. M.F.H., R.L.-S., M.N. and L.K. performed whole-mount stainings and imaging. M.F.H., K.K. and S.K. performed the flow cytometry experiments and analysis of immune cells. R.L.-S., D.C. and I.C.-A. performed the flow cytometry and image stream experiments and analysis of epithelial cells. L.K., A.M.F. and M.F.H. performed the cytokine measurements. N.A., S.R.V., Y.B. and J.B. generated the organoid reporter lines. J.F., A.A. and C.S. performed and processed the proteomic measurements. Live imaging was performed by M.F.H., R.L.-S. and M.N., and analysed by M.B. M.H. and D.B. generated and provided the S.Tm strains. T.R. and F.G. supported with data interpretation. All authors read and approved the manuscript.

a) Picture of a chip-slide with culture medium, including a 3D-rendered image of the cross-section of the chip-slide containing three individual chip segments and an image of the micropatterned stamp with a representative bright-field image of an engineered intestine cross-section, e > 15. b) Time course of biomimetic epithelium formation from the stamped empty ECM to epithelium coverage and maturation. Scale bars: 500 µm. c) Quantification of viable crypts of 16 donors from duodenum, ileum and colon, d = 16. d) Representative EDF brightfield image of a Z-stack, showing the top-view of a day-9 epithelium, e = 3. Scale bar: 200 µm. The magnified insert (top) highlights a 3D-reconstruction of the epithelium with crypts penetrating into the matrix. The magnified insert (bottom) shows an EDF image of a Z-stack in the crypt area. Scale bar: 50 µm. e) Representative EDF fluorescent image of selected Z-stacks with magnified insert, showing an iCas9 CDH1-mScarlet3 day-9 duodenal epithelium with tight E-Cadherin+ adherens junctions (red), e = 6. Scale bar: 100 µm. f) Overview of the high-throughput histo-processing workflow using 3D-printed histomold facilitating co-planar embedding of up to fifty engineered epithelia at once. Post-FFPE embedding, dozens of engineered epithelia can be visualized within one section as illustrated in a representative H&E. Consecutive sections subjected to H&E and mIF to evaluate the spatial organization and maturation of a duodenal epithelium at day 6. Scale bar: 100 µm. g) H&E cross-sections of representative colon engineered epithelium and primary tissue, showing high morphological similarity, crypt depth, and goblet cell distribution, e = 5. Scale bars: 100 µm.

a-c) Representative mIF cross-section of engineered duodenal, ileal and colonic epithelia in direct comparison to the donor-matched primary tissue (ileum not matched), highlighting the stem-niche specific SOX9+ (cyan) and transit-amplifying Ki67+ cells (pink), matching abundance of MUC2+ goblet cells (green) and high expression of the region-enriched absorptive lineage marker (orange) in the E-Cadherin+ epithelium (grey). The duodenal epithelium was marked by strong expression APOA4+ enterocytes, matching the parental tissue. Expression of distal FABP6+ enterocytes in the top-layer of the engineered epithelium matched ileal tissue. The colonic epithelium exhibited CA1+ colonocytes at comparable levels to the organ of origin, e = 4. Scale bars: 50 µm.

a) Representative H&E images of engineered duodenal epithelia over 10 days of maturation, highlighting epithelial polarization, thickening, and increasing crypt depth, e = 3. Scale bar: 50 µm. b) Representative mIF images of spatiotemporal patterning of SOX9+ (cyan) and Ki67+ (red) cells of E-Cadherin+ (orange) duodenal epithelium over 10 days, e = 3. Scale bar: 100 µm. c) Representative mIF showcasing crypt and top layer annotations and cell segmentation with respective masks for SOX9+ (cyan) and Ki67+ cells (red), e = 3. Scale bar: 100 µm. d) Quantification of SOX9+ cells in the respective annotation across multiple time points, normalized to overall DAPI+ cell count in the annotation. e) Quantification of Ki67+ cells in the respective annotation over time, normalized to overall DAPI+ cell count in the annotation. Line plots in d-e) represent the mean of donors (d = 3) ± SD at day 9, derived from three tissues per donor. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test (ns=P > 0.05). f) Average epithelial thickness in donor-matched duodenal tissue and engineered epithelia. Bars represent the mean of donors (d = 3) ± SD (dots), derived from regions of engineered epithelia (n = 3) per donor and matched primary tissue (dots). #72428. Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5188 w)

Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.
  • According to recent reports, they swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under latest manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect.
  • City created enough space for themselves through clever movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.

According to recent reports, they swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under latest manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect. The Frenchman’s two goals included a captivating mazy dribble, which will long be remembered by those who had the fortune to see it.

City created enough space for themselves through clever movement. With Cherki zigging one way and Phil Foden zagging the other, they created even more by dribbling past a mesmerised Palace back three that became a back five at times and still could not cope.

Erling Haaland also scored twice. Even with the creative and unpredictable talents of those behind in a four-man attacking City midfield, Haaland remains irreplaceable with his ability to convert chances.

Industry observers note that however, this night belonged to Cherki. Guardiola chided him publicly after he set up a City goal with a “rabona” cross last season. The thrust of Guardiola’s comments were that Cherki was not Lionel Messi. Of course not, but he possesses a genius all of his own, which Maresca would surely be foolish to rein in.

The jaw-dropping splendour of Cherki’s first goal drew a collective intake of breath at Selhurst Park.

Collecting a Foden pass, he attacked the Palace area on a diagonal path, slaloming between Jaydee Canvot, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chris Richards, before having the spatial awareness and technique to flick his left foot at the ball to send it rolling on a perpendicular trajectory past Dean Henderson.

"The man with the magic feet!"Rayan Cherki doubles Manchester City's lead with a STUNNING goal 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/9Zea5vFljv.

An insight into Cherki’s mindset came after the match.

Recent findings suggest that he said: “My performance is s---. In the first half, we didn’t find the space, I played bad. I need to show them that I want to play, I want to score. Next time I want to give the ball around more.”.

Forget the words, Maresca cannot ignore the actions of a player he left on the bench against Bournemouth.

Sterner tests will come for City than against a Palace side missing key players who may or may not leave south London in the remaining days of the transfer window.

Whether Maresca will trust his forward players to express themselves as freely against their rivals for the Premier League title remains to be seen, but with Elliot Anderson providing a one-man shield behind them, City could not be stopped.

Maresca stated: “For sure Rayan is happy tonight. His performance was very good and not just for his two goals. He has to press off the ball and he was in charge of [marking] Adam Wharton, so it was a complete game by him.”.

Only for the first three minutes did Palace hint at a different outcome but, after shots from Eddie Nketiah and Daichi Kamada were diverted away for corners, City took control.

They took the lead in the 17th minute when the otherwise quiet Antoine Semenyo flighted a cross over the heads of everyone except the shorn locks of Haaland, whose determined header looped over Henderson and dropped in the far corner.

The only negative of Foden’s performance came in front of goal, with a ballooned shot and a mistimed header.

After Cherki’s solo masterpiece had made it 2-0, Yeremy Pino seized the next moment for his own with a stunning free-kick that flicked the crossbar, then the back of City keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma before finally dropping over the line.

"This is a good a free-kick as you're likely to see this season!" Yéremy Pino's stirke beats Donnarumma 🎯 pic.twitter.com/5uF4vzOXDp.

Whatever hope that mustered was snatched away again when Cherki scored his second goal and the third goal of a breathless five minutes.

His shot at the end of a darting run flicked the ankle of Tomiyasu to send it just out of Henderson’s reach.

In a recent development, rayan Cherki AGAIN! Manchester City have breathing room once again after another strike from the Frenchman 👏 pic.twitter.com/Tyw9whPS2r.

Morocco teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi had little time to show why City have paid Lille £85.6m for him with a late entry as a substitute, but they didn’t need him on this occasion.

Foden then set off on a swerving run that set up Haaland to lash home his second goal of the game and make it 4-1.

Erling Haaland scores gets another! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/4mz2eF7wFF.

The fear for Palace is that they cannot keep selling their best players and expecting to replicate the success on the pitch that has brought them three trophies in the past 15 months.

Leicester City offer a shuddering example of that. From Premier League champions to League One in 10 seasons.

Pierre Sage, the new Palace manager, will welcome the certainty that the closure of the transfer window will bring, particularly over the futures of forwards Ismaïla Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, as well as wing-back Daniel Muñoz.

The one player he cannot afford to lose is Wharton, who matched the City midfield on his own at times in the first half.

According to recent reports, sage remarked: “I think the score is heavy. We stayed in the game for 65 minutes and created some chances. We know we are in for a tough season, but we have created a lot of opportunities in the first two games.

“I could speak about the transfer window, but I don’t want to find an excuse. We just have to be sure that in four days’ time, the team will be better than today.”.

“It has been a short pre-season. Rayan [Cherki], five weeks ago was at the World Cup. Game by game, we will be back, just need a few games. We played well, it is a fresh manager but we have been playing together, with the addition of a few new players. We know what to do and have to trust the system.”.

Sources indicate that “We have to keep on playing together, find out where we are best and how to play. We have so many good players and we have to fit everyone in. He has to keep going because we know how good Phil is, it is about showing it week in week out. This is the right step forward for everyone. We have to build on this.”.

"I'm just trying to play my football" 💪Elliot Anderson is excited about the future at Manchester City after his summer transfer 🔥 pic.twitter.com/huGv4Li3GZ.

"Say what you actually mean!" 🤣Erling Haaland takes over Rayan Cherki's post-match interview! pic.twitter.com/adW6IU8DzQ.

Industry observers note that 2 + 2 - Rayan Cherki is the third player to have a game with multiple goals and another game with multiple assists across a team's first two matches of a Premier League campaign, after Thierry Henry in 2004-05 and Didier Drogba in 2010-11.Polymath. pic.twitter.com/4cRV0xMIFa.

September 5: Fulham vs Crystal PalaceSeptember 12: Crystal Palace vs IpswichSeptember 19: Leeds vs Crystal PalaceOctober 11: Crystal Palace vs Nottingham ForestOctober 18: Brighton vs Crystal Palace.

Pierre Sage’s side will host Middlesbrough in the League Cup third round next month and will also begin their Europa League campaign in September.

The directions of these teams will be diverging this season. City were wonderful, free-flowing, expressive and fun to watch. Palace not so much. It will take Pierre Sage a while to impose his style of play. It will certainly take another week before he knows his final squad for the first half of the season.

It was noticeable at the final whistle that many Palace fans stayed around to applaud Daniel Munoz, an unused substitute on the night, as he made his way to the tunnel, probably for the final time as a Palace player if Nottingham Forest’s interest in him becomes a transfer by the end of the window.

"Cherki was the difference" 🪄"He is a genius" 🧠Jamie Redknapp reacts to Crystal Palace 1-4 Man City 🔊 pic.twitter.com/UjSarMngDR.

Manchester City will take on Norwich in the League Cup third round in September and will also have their first Champions League match next month.

Pretty comprehensive in Manchester City’s favour, which is reflected in the scoreline.

The final whistle is blown at Selhurst Park and Manchester City have cruised to a 4-1 win thanks to doubles from Cherki and Haaland. Enzo Maresca’s side make it two wins from two whereas it is two defeats from two for Pierre Sage.

Sources indicate that manchester City, with the three points already in the bag, are just stroking the ball around with ease and are in complete control. Palace can barely get a foot on it.

There will be five added minutes.

In a recent development, A late double substitution for Manchester City as Reis and Braithwaite come on. Enzo Maresca’s side are cruising to victory to make it two wins from two.

Cherki has two goals to his name and now Haaland does as Manchester City are romping to victory in south London. Guehi wins possession for City inside the Palace half and the ball comes to Foden, who dribbles towards the Palace penalty area. He lays it off to his left to Haaland who, from a narrow angle, finds the root of the net.

Erling Haaland scores gets another! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/4mz2eF7wFF.

Nearly an instant impact from McAidoo as the 18-year-old drives through the Palace half and curls a shot from the edge of the box that goes just wide.

When Manchester City were making those substitutions, the Crystal Palace fans were making sure they let the officials know how long the Manchester City players were taking to get off.

Recent findings suggest that there is going to be a debut for the Premier League’s most expensive teenager ever as Bouaddi comes on for Manchester City. McAidoo is also coming on, with Cherki and Anderson going off.

According to recent reports, mingueza eventually comes on but not after having to wait until the ball goes out of play again as Khalaili was adjudged to have taken too long to have got off the pitch. Safe to say the Palace fans are not too impressed with that newly introduced rule. It will probably be a pub question in the years ahead. That change does mean that Palace have used all five substitutions, which means Munoz will not come on. He is being linked with a reunion with Oliver Glasner at Nottingham Forest in the final days of this window.

Crystal Palace make another double change and it will be two debuts as Disasi and Mingueza come on.

Enzo Maresca turns to his bench for the first time tonight as Kovacic comes on.

Khalaili brings down Semenyo and is booked for that challenge.

Palace are going to make a double substitution as McNeil and Gozo replace Nketiah and Pino. 19-year-old Gozo is on for his Palace debut.

Recent findings suggest that that was a chance for Palace. Guessand finds Pino, who drives into the Manchester City penalty area on the right. Pino has Nketiah at the far post but there is too much on the cross.

Guessand, back at Palace, is going to come on to replace Strand Larsen, who has been pretty quiet up top for the home side tonight.

Sources indicate that sometimes you feel blessed to witness an extraordinary moment of footballing genius. Selhurst Park has just seen two in the space of three minutes. Yeremy Pino’s free-kick which flicked off the back of Gianluigi Donnarumma was stunning, but even that could not truly compare to the slalom run of Rayan Cherki that drew a collective intake of breath from all those present. The Frenchman has just followed it with a scorching shot. It couldn’t compare with his first, though.

According to recent reports, three goals come in quick succession and Cherki restores Manchester City’s two-goal advantage with his second of the night. The Frenchman receives it on the turn from around 30 yards out and drives towards the Palace penalty area. He then shoots and a kind deflection off Richards takes it over Henderson’s diving effort and into the Palace net.

Sources indicate that rayan Cherki AGAIN! Manchester City have breathing room once again after another strike from the Frenchman 👏 pic.twitter.com/Tyw9whPS2r.

Just as the hosts appeared to maybe out of this one, they get a goal back. Pino’s fantastic free-kick strikes the bar, hits Donnarumma on the back before going into the net off the post. That hit the frame of the goal twice and Palace have a crucial goal, minutes after going 2-0 down.

"This is a good a free-kick as you're likely to see this season!" Yéremy Pino's stirke beats Donnarumma 🎯 pic.twitter.com/5uF4vzOXDp.

Anderson brings down Pino not far outside the Manchester City penalty area and is booked.

Pino is lining up the free-kick...

The next goal in this game felt crucial and the visitors have it. Foden drives towards the Palace penalty area before playing a pass forward into the path of Cherki. The Frenchman has numerous defenders around but he indicates neat footwork to skip past a few, holds off Richards before slotting home with his left foot.

"The man with the magic feet!"Rayan Cherki doubles Manchester City's lead with a STUNNING goal 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/9Zea5vFljv.

No-one has had fewer touches on the pitch tonight than Haaland up until this point but the Norwegian’s goal is the difference. His number of touches (14) is the joint fewest with his compatriot Strand Larsen.

In a recent development, that was a good chance for Nketiah. He plays the ball to the underlapping Mitchell, who from the byline cuts it back into the path of Nketiah. The former Arsenal man should so so much better with his opportunity from the edge of the six-yard box but fires a long way wide.

Recent findings suggest that semenyo wins Manchester City an early corner in this second half off Canvot. Anderson’s delivery beyond the back post picks out O’Reilly, who in space heads back across goal but Pino heads away.

We are back under way at Selhurst Park, with Manchester City carrying a 1-0 lead into this second half. As the players emerged from the tunnels for the second half, the DJ at Selhurst Park paid tribute to the late Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers by playing Islands in the Stream. Nice touch! Get your favourite Dolly and Kenny tunes in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

No changes for either side at the break.

The stats are certainly in Manchester City’s favour and they will feel they probably should have more than the one goal.

Cherki has a late chance for Manchester City but his shot is well saved by Henderson down to his right.

The first half at Selhurst Park is then brought to an end and Manchester City lead 1-0 at the break thanks to Haaland’s header.

There will be just one added minute at the end of this first half.

Palace started off with a nominal back three. That has become a back five far too often for Pierre Sage’s liking at times in this first half, yet still City are playing through them almost at will. The Palace fans whose deafening support accompanied Palace shots in the opening minutes are reduced to cheering battling midfield runs that win a free-kick now.

Sources indicate that pino delivers a free-kick into the Manchester City box and Richards gets to it first. It comes off his shoulder and rolls into the arms of Donnarumma.

Semenyo’s shot from the left side of the box takes a deflection off Richards, forcing Henderson into a decent save.

Palace now miss a big opportunity and should be on level terms. Wharton, who has probably been the best player on the pitch tonight, whips in a cross from the right and picks out Mitchell, who has a free header from eight yards out but somehow misses the target.

Strand Larsen comes close with a header from a Pino cross but he would have been offside anyway.

The first booking of the night goes the way of the visitors. Wharton drives forward into the Manchester City half and is cynically brought down by Cherki, who looked perplexed when the yellow card was shown but it was an obvious booking.

It has been revealed that foden wastes his second major chance of this first half. Manchester City break through O’Reilly, who carries it down the right. He waits for Cherki to make the overlapping run before passing to the Frenchman. Cherki’s cross picks out Foden inside the six-yard box and the latter should score but he gets a simple header all wrong.

Well, that was easy. So easy in fact – perfect Semenyo cross, perfect Haaland header - that it hushed Selhurst Park as the ball looped over Dean Henderson. Even the roar from the enclave of City fans took a moment to fill the south London air. You wouldn’t say that all the pre-match optimism among Palace fans has been punctured, but the home side need a moment if they aren’t to sink without trace to a City side bossing possession and territory now.

Sources indicate that that is a huge miss from Foden. Anderson picks out his compatriot in acres of space on the right side of the box, with no Palace defender within five yards of him, but Foden blazes over the bar when he should have put Manchester City 2-0 up.

King Harald V of Norway has died in the last few days and over the last few hours two Norwegian cyclists claimed a one-two at the Vuelta a Espana and now Haaland has a goal.

According to recent reports, he has barely touched the ball thus far but he puts the visitors ahead just past the quarter-of-an-hour mark. Semenyo is afforded too much space on the left just outside the penalty area and clips in a cross towards the far post. Haaland gets up highest, above Richards, and guides a superb header over Henderson into the Palace net.

Erling Haaland gets off the mark for the latest Premier League season! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/5ZjQUVk6Zl.

The England boss is in attendance tonight, perhaps keeping a close eye on that midfield battle between Anderson and Wharton.

Palace flirt with danger inside their own penalty area. After Haaland’s flick, Kamada should just belt the ball away but instead inexplicably leaves it. Henderson manages to mop up just as Foden was eyeing up the chance.

According to recent reports, there is a mad scramble inside the Palace box but somehow the hosts escape without conceding. Initially, Anderson’s shot from range is saved by Henderson but Manchester City keep it alive in the penalty area. Palace frantically attempt to clear their lines and eventually they do after Haaland came close.

Industry observers note that quite a lot of the focus tonight will be on two English midfielders; one who has got a big-money move this summer and the other thus far has not. Anderson is directly up against Wharton and so far it is the latter who is winning the early battles, including dispossessing Anderson in midfield.

The first chance of the game goes the way of the hosts. It stems from a quite sensational first-time pass from Wharton from inside his own half into the left channel to pick out the run of Nketiah, whose shot from the left side of the box takes a deflection off Dias and is saved by Donnarumma.

Sources indicate that manchester City initially clear the corner but Palace keep it alive. Kamada’s shot from just inside the box appeared to be on target but it is headed over for another corner, which is easily caught by Donnarumma.

We are under way at Selhurst Park. Will Pierre Sage earn his first win as Palace boss or can Enzo Maresca and City make it two wins from two?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel in the corner of Selhurst Park to the customary sound of Glad All Over and we are moments away from kick-off in south London. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:.

Recent findings suggest that yes! It may have been fleeting but the boy in the Palace tracksuit top had his moment after all with Erling Haaland as City waited in line to enter the Selhurst Park pitch. And having done so, he fairly skipped up the steps back with his dad back to their seats. Whether the boy’s second wish of the evening, for a Palace victory, will come true is another question altogether.

According to recent reports, the young Palace fan is still waiting for Haaland. Another determined walk back to the dressing room. It isn’t a simple task to attract an opposition player’s attention when you are leaning over a barrier a few feet higher than him – and in the home end. Haaland and his teammates have the look of a team that knows it must perform tonight to ease the concerns that they are a team in transition. The City fans will not entertain such thoughts, either.

Crystal Palace looked set to sign Club Brugge defender Joel Ordonez but that deal could be in doubt as there may be some problems with his medical. We await to see further updates on that situation.

“He is a genius. Make no mistake. Managers now want structure, they do not like players who are a bit loose out of possession. But I go to football matches to watch people like him play.

“That is what makes me smile. I do not like watching players pass it sideways, that is not why I go to football. I go to watch geniuses do their work. Some managers will not appreciate it. But last week he got his manager out of a hole because without him they would not have won that game.”.

"He's irreplaceable" 💥Jamie Redknapp and Clinton Morrison sing the praises of Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton 🤝 pic.twitter.com/ZOpcZcItHY.

It has been revealed that jack Grealish is not in the Manchester City squad tonight amid links with the likes of Everton and Sunderland. Will he still be at the club beyond the deadline? It would appear not.

Both Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta are out of the Crystal Palace squad tonight with injury but could they be on the move before the window slams shut? Sarr has been linked with Galatasaray and Liverpool whilst the situation is complicated with Mateta as he claims the final year of his contract is void. How do those two situations resolve themselves? Daniel Munoz has been linked with a move to Nottingham Forest but is on the bench for Palace this evening.

Industry observers note that an unfulfilled wish so far for a young Palace fan holding up a child’s red Norway shirt with ‘Haaland’ emblazoned on it. Having waited patiently for the City players to emerge for their warm-up and being held by his dad as he leant over the stone wall to attract Haaland’s attention, he was left disappointed because the City striker was simply not looking as he and his teammates jogged past. Will the boy, who has on a Palace tracksuit top, get a photo with his hero when the striker returns to the Portakabin that hosts the away dressing room prior to kick-off? Stay tuned.

There looks set to be a debut for the Premier League’s most expensive teenager off the visitors’ bench in the form of Ayyoub Bouaddi. There is no Jack Grealish in their squad as his future is up in the air.

Manchester City: Donnarumma, Khusanov, Dias, Gvardiol, O’Reilly, Anderson, Guehi, Cherki, Foden Semenyo, Haaland.Substitutes: Rulli, Kovacic, Ait-Nouri, Reis, Echeverri, Bouaddi, McAidoo, Braithwaite, Lewis.

Recent findings suggest that was it really just a year ago when Crystal Palace fans flooded down the Holmesdale Road with not a care in the world having just won the Community Shield to add to their FA Cup triumph over tonight’s opponents Manchester City? Well, they are marching along the Holmesdale Road in the same numbers again this evening, bedecked in red and blue as always, yet there is uncertainty and worry in the air and on their faces. Will the player exodus continue? What should they make of new manager Pierre Sage? Will the good times fade from view as quickly as they did for Leicester City or can Sage build a new side to match the one which, under Oliver Glasner, added the Conference League to their list of trophies three months ago?

“We struggled to get into the game and win the battles,” a disappointed Carlo Ancelotti lamented.

Industry observers note that at the World Cup, an industrious 18-year-old showed maturity beyond his years to dominate the midfield against Ancelotti’s Brazil on his competitive international debut, earning Morocco a draw. That was, in fact, the second time an Ancelotti side had been undone by precocious teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Ancelotti’s remarks about losing the midfield battle are from after a Champions League match in October 2024, when Lille shocked Real Madrid to end their 36-game unbeaten run. Bouaddi was at the heart of both statement results for his club and country.

Tonight:Crystal Palace vs Manchester City.

Saturday:Liverpool vs Nottingham ForestBournemouth vs EvertonCoventry vs Hull CityTottenham vs Newcastle.

Sunday:Chelsea vs BrightonLeeds vs BrentfordSunderland vs FulhamManchester United vs Ipswich.

Recent findings suggest that tonight's team to face Crystal Palace! ​​💪🩵XI | Donnarumma, Khusanov, Dias (C), Gvardiol, O'Reilly, Anderson, Guéhi, Foden, Cherki, Semenyo, HaalandSUBS | Rulli, Kovačić, Aït-Nouri, Reis, Echeverri, Bouaddi, McAidoo, Braithwaite, Lewis🤝 @etihad pic.twitter.com/qNgJPXKDM7.

COYP. 🦅 pic.twitter.com/78ZUj8SBOf.

The second weekend of the Premier League season kicks off under the lights in South London as Crystal Palace host Manchester City at Selhurst Park. Manchester City won both fixtures 3-0 last season and they are in fact unbeaten in their last 11 Premier league away games against Crystal Palace, who have won just two of the 22 top flight meetings.

In a recent development, crystal Palace experienced defeat on the opening weekend, falling to a 2-0 loss at Everton last Saturday, meaning the Pierre Sage era started with a defeat. Tonight is Sage’s first home game in charge of the club.

“I think it will be a wonderful moment, but I prefer to have a wonderful moment with good news at the end of the game,” Sage said. “That is why I do not think about me in this situation. The most important thing is the team and the result for sure, because we prepare all the week for that, to make them [the fans] happy. They will be happy to see us, but I think they would prefer to see us win. I will give my life to make them happy. I cannot do more. When you are in this stadium [Selhurst Park], you feel the history. You feel that there is something heavy weighing on you. It is a great responsibility that I have been entrusted with. We cannot wait to see this stadium in action.”.

Sage has confirmed that Ismaila Sarr, who has been linked with a move away from the club this summer, and Chadi Riad will miss out tonight due to injury, as will striker Jean-Philippe Mateta. Palace have confirmed the addition of Axel Disasi on loan from Chelsea and the French defender could be involved tonight.

Manchester City appeared to be heading towards defeat in Enzo Maresca’s first league game in charge of the club last weekend. They were 1-0 down at home against Bournemouth in the closing stages before goals from Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol gave them a come-from-behind win.

In a recent development, it has been a busy week in the transfer window for Manchester City. Both Savio (formerly Savinho) and Omar Marmoush have left for Tottenham, joining a long list of departures from the Etihad this summer. Moroccan midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi has arrived in an £85m deal from Lille and has become the most expensive teenager in Premier League history. Maresca has confirmed that 18-year-old Bouaddi is ready to start.

“He [Bouaddi] is ready,” Maresca said. “He was working with his former club so he is fit. We will see how long he needs in terms of adaptation but he is ready to go. He is quite calm. He does not look 18, he already looks older, which is important. But in this case, we need to go slowly because he is very young, he has come from a different country so there is no rush for him. He is going to help us now and in the future. He is very mature for being 18.”.

Team news from Selhurst Park to follow shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carlo Pellegatti has painted a positive picture regarding AC Milan’s developments, one that puts last season’s collapse into perspective.

Rewinding to the end of May, it felt like Milan’s entire world have caved in. A 2-1 defeat at home to Cagliari – a game that they led in early on – in the final round of the season condemned the Rossoneri to a fifth-placed finish, meaning they missed out on Champions League football again.

According to recent reports, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This is after Massimiliano Allegri had the team in a title fight going into the Spring, but ultimately the decline was near-vertical towards the end of the campaign. He paid the price for this, as did the CEO Giorgio Furlani, sporting director Igli Tare and chief scout Geoffrey Moncada.

In his latest column for MilanNews, Carlo Pellegatti has put forward the notion that the defeat to the Sardinians might turn out to be a blessing. Why? Because the reset that followed on a sporting and managerial level seems to already be taking a positive shape.

According to recent reports, “Krosche and delight! It’s a somewhat obvious joke, but it captures the expectations of AC Milan fans. When will he arrive? November 27th, as I’ve been told, or in the first ten days of December, or even – I really hope not – January 1st?” he began.

“The difference in dates for the announcement of his upcoming role is by no means insignificant, because the January transfer window becomes a crucial turning point for Milan’s fortunes, both today and in the future.

“The sooner the Head of Football sits down at Casa Milan, the better he can weave his web to strengthen the team in the winter transfer window. This should have been the job of a year ago, but was not accomplished by a shortsighted management team that never understood the difference between costs and investments.

It has been revealed that “It’s also a shame that Igli Tare is a person who respects roles and is attentive to internal balances. He had to, and this is his great regret, bypass those who managed Milan, to speak with Gerry Cardinale and explain the importance of the arrival of a striker and a defender, who would have allowed them to be in the Champions League today.

“I’m using a very bold paradox, one I’ve never admitted. If failing to qualify for the Champions League was the reason that pushed Gerry Cardinale to fire the key figures of the three worst and most disastrous years in Milan’s history, then, given the exciting future prospects, it would have been better to lose against Cagliari, which avoided prolonging the agony of our dear old AC Milan. A painful sacrifice that, I hope, will be repaid with success in the years to come.

“With a Cardinale who was too absent and distant, guilty, by his own admission, of having delegated the management of his club to unsuitable people, but who now becomes the protagonist of this new way of operating, reminiscent of the good old days.

“I obviously feel sorry for Tare and Allegri, who, despite having their responsibilities, were victims of a confusing, chaotic, and divisive situation, and through no fault of their own.

In a recent development, “Returning to Krosche, I hope he quickly finds his feet in this Milan adventure that awaits him. I continue to believe that a highly experienced and highly skilled Italian operative, to work alongside the German director, could and can be of help to him and Milan, given the obvious difficulties of integrating into a world that is completely different from the German one.

Recent findings suggest that “Gerry Cardinale and his chief assistant, Massimo Calvelli, are convinced of the wisdom of their choice, after meeting several times with Markus Krosche. I think it’s crucial that he’s not only a skilled market operator, but also a valid on-field contact for Ruben Amorim.

“The Portuguese will then be able to discuss potential choices and decisions with his Head of Football. In short, it was a position in the organisational chart that was culpably neglected, with the results that were seen, until Gerry Cardinale himself imposed Igli Tare, who, in any case, did not have an easy job.

“I mentioned Massimo Calvelli, who, in the media, always appears to be somewhat out of the spotlight. Certainly not in operational terms, because, from what I know, he was the absolute protagonist and architect of transactions that brought approximately €825m into Milan’s coffers.

“He was certainly a skilled architect of the return of Adidas as a shirt sponsor, but also a key figure in the acquisition of Generali, which will give its name to the latest stadium, this time with the collaboration, it is said, of Paolo Scaroni.

“Therefore, he is a valuable executive who works behind the scenes, but with excellent results in terms of economic and financial aspects and also for the club’s image.”.
